steps.detail: Rearrange one equation so a letter stands alone, substitute that whole expression into the other, and solve the single-variable equation that results. Put the value back into the simplest equation to get the second letter. Check both equations, not one.
steps.proof: x = 2 and y = 5, and both original equations hold.
steps.pitfall: Finding x and stopping, when the question asked for the point.

steps.title: Solve a Pair by Elimination
steps.mastery: Solve simultaneous equations by scaling and adding to cancel one variable.
steps.practice: Solve 3x + 2y = 16 together with 5x - 2y = 8.
steps.detail: Line the equations up in columns. If a variable has equal and opposite coefficients, add; if they are equal and the same sign, subtract. Scale one or both equations first when neither matches. Elimination is quicker than substitution whenever nothing is already isolated.
steps.proof: x = 3 and y = 3.5.
steps.pitfall: Adding when the coefficients match in sign, so nothing actually cancels.

steps.title: Place Them on a Line
steps.mastery: Order positive and negative numbers and read distances between them.
steps.practice: Order -7, 3, -2, 0 and -10 from smallest to largest, then find the distance from -7 to 3.
steps.detail: Further left is smaller, always. The distance between two points is the difference, and it is never negative. Drawing the line and marking the numbers takes twenty seconds and removes the whole class of ordering mistakes.
steps.proof: -10, -7, -2, 0, 3, and the distance is 10.
steps.pitfall: Ranking -10 above -2 because 10 is bigger than 2.

problems.prompt: Order -3, 1 and -7 from smallest to largest.
Order -7, 3, -2, 0 and -10 from smallest to largest.
On a number line, find the distance from -7 to 3, and from -12 to -4.
problems.answer: 10 and 8, and neither distance can be negative.

steps.title: Add and Subtract Signs
steps.mastery: Handle a minus sign that sits next to another sign without guessing.
steps.practice: Work out 5 - (-3) and -4 + 7, then say which of the two signs cancelled.
steps.detail: Subtracting a negative is adding. Rewrite every double sign as a single one before you compute anything: 5 - (-3) becomes 5 + 3. Addition of a negative is subtraction, so -4 + 7 is 7 - 4 with the sign of the larger magnitude.
steps.proof: 8 and 3; the double minus in the first became a plus.
steps.pitfall: Reading -6 - 2 as -4 by treating the second minus as a subtraction of a negative.

problems.prompt: Compute 5 - (-3).
Compute -4 + 7 and -6 - 2.
problems.answer: 3 and -8.

problems.hint: Rewrite every double sign as a single one first.

steps.title: Multiply and Divide Signs
steps.mastery: Determine the sign of a product or quotient from the signs of its parts.
steps.practice: Multiply -6 by -4, divide -20 by 5, then find the sign of -2 x 3 x -5.
steps.detail: Two negatives multiply to a positive; one negative gives a negative. With more than two factors, count the negatives — an even count is positive, an odd count is negative. Work out the sign first and the magnitude second, and they cannot contaminate each other.
steps.proof: 24, then -4, and the triple product is positive at 30.
steps.pitfall: Applying the addition rules to multiplication, so -6 x -4 comes out as -24.

problems.prompt: Compute -6 x -4.
Compute -20 divided by 5, then -2 x 3 x -5.
Give the sign of (-2) x (-3) x (-4) x (-5) without computing, then give the value.
problems.answer: Positive, because there are four negatives. The value is 120.

steps.title: Powers of Negatives
steps.mastery: Evaluate a negative base raised to a power, brackets included.
steps.practice: Evaluate (-3)^2, then -3^2, then (-2)^3.
steps.detail: Without brackets the exponent binds to the 3 and the minus sign is applied afterwards, so -3^2 is -(3^2). With brackets the whole negative number is squared. An even power of a negative is positive; an odd power keeps the sign.
steps.pitfall: Treating -3^2 and (-3)^2 as the same expression.

problems.prompt: Evaluate (-3)^2.
Evaluate -3^2 and (-2)^3.
Evaluate (-1)^99 and (-2)^4, and state the rule you used for the sign.
problems.answer: -1 and 16. An odd power keeps the sign; an even power makes it positive.

steps.title: Signs Inside Algebra
steps.mastery: Expand and simplify an expression where negatives sit inside brackets.
steps.practice: Expand and simplify 4 - 2(3x - 5) and -(x - 7) + 2x.
steps.detail: The sign in front of a bracket belongs to every term inside it. Write the multiplier with its sign attached — here it is -2, not 2 — and distribute that. A bare minus in front of a bracket is a multiplier of -1 and flips every term.
steps.pitfall: Distributing the 2 but not the minus sign, so -2(3x - 5) becomes -6x - 10.

problems.prompt: Expand 4(2x - 3).
Expand and simplify 4 - 2(3x - 5).
Expand and simplify -(x - 7) + 2x - 3(1 - x).
problems.hint: The bare minus in front of the first bracket is a multiplier of -1.

steps.title: Read the Convention
steps.mastery: State the agreed order of evaluation and why one is needed at all.
steps.practice: Evaluate 2 + 3 x 4 and 6 - 2 - 1, and say which convention decided each.
steps.detail: Brackets, then indices, then multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction. The last two pairs are equal in rank and settle left to right. That second half is the part people skip, and it is what makes 6 - 2 - 1 come out as 3 rather than 5.
steps.proof: 14 and 3, from precedence and from left-to-right association.
steps.pitfall: Treating left-to-right as the whole rule, which turns 2 + 3 x 4 into 20.

problems.prompt: Evaluate 2 + 3 x 4.
Evaluate 6 - 2 - 1 and say which rule fixes the order.
problems.answer: 3, by left-to-right association.

problems.prompt: Evaluate 20 - 3 x 4 + 8 / 2 and list the order you applied the operations in.
problems.answer: 12: the product 12 and the quotient 4 first, then 20 - 12 + 4 left to right.

steps.title: Nested Brackets
steps.mastery: Evaluate an expression with brackets inside brackets, innermost first.
steps.practice: Evaluate 3 x (4 + 2 x (5 - 3)) - 7 by working from the innermost bracket outwards.
steps.detail: Rewrite the whole expression after each bracket closes rather than editing it in place. It costs three extra lines and removes the step where you lose track of which bracket you are inside. Count the opening and closing brackets before you start.
steps.proof: The answer is 17: the inner bracket is 2, then 4 + 4 = 8, then 24 - 7.
steps.pitfall: Starting at the leftmost bracket rather than the innermost one.

problems.prompt: Evaluate 2 x (5 - 3).
Evaluate 5 x (2 + 3 x (6 - 4)) - 9.
Evaluate 2 x (3 + (8 - (4 - 1))) and write the expression out again after each bracket closes.

steps.title: Powers Before Products
steps.mastery: Apply an exponent before any multiplication or division around it.
steps.practice: Evaluate 2 x 3^2 and (2 x 3)^2, and say why they differ.
steps.detail: An exponent attaches to the single thing immediately under it, not to everything to its left. Writing the implied bracket in — 2 x (3^2) — settles the question every time. The same reasoning covers -3^2, which is -9 rather than 9.
steps.proof: 18 and 36 — the exponent binds to the 3 alone in the first, to the product in the second.
steps.pitfall: Reading 2 x 3^2 as (2 x 3)^2 because the multiplication is written first.

problems.prompt: Evaluate 3^2 and (-3)^2.
problems.answer: 9 and 9.

problems.prompt: Evaluate 4 x 2^3 and (4 x 2)^3, and state which number the exponent attaches to in each.
problems.answer: 32 and 512. In the first it attaches to the 2 alone; in the second to the whole product.

problems.prompt: Evaluate -3^2 + (-3)^2 and explain the two different signs.
problems.answer: 0. The first is -(3^2) = -9, the second is 9.

steps.title: Implied Brackets in Fractions
steps.mastery: Recognise that a fraction bar groups its whole numerator and denominator.
steps.practice: Evaluate (8 + 4) / (3 + 1) and compare it with 8 + 4 / 3 + 1.
steps.detail: A horizontal bar is a bracket you cannot see. The moment the expression goes on one line, those brackets have to be written. This is the single most common transcription error when copying working into a calculator, and it is silent.
steps.proof: The first is 3; the second is about 10.33, because only the 4 is divided.
steps.pitfall: Typing a written fraction into a calculator without bracketing the numerator and denominator.

problems.prompt: Evaluate (8 + 4) / (3 + 1).
Evaluate 12 / (2 + 4) and 12 / 2 + 4, and say which one the written fraction 12 over (2+4) means.
problems.answer: 2 and 10. The written fraction means the first.

problems.prompt: Write the fraction with numerator 5 + 7 over denominator 2 x 3 on a single line, then evaluate it.
problems.answer: It must be bracketed as (5 + 7) / (2 x 3), which comes to 2.
problems.hint: An unbracketed 5 + 7 / 2 x 3 gives 15.5 instead.

steps.title: Rebuild a Wrong Answer
steps.mastery: Locate which precedence step an incorrect evaluation went wrong at.
steps.practice: Somebody evaluated 10 - 2 x 3 + 4 as 28. Say which step they took first.
steps.detail: Work the expression yourself, then compare line by line against theirs until the two diverge. The first line that differs is the error, and naming it — precedence, association, a sign — is what stops it recurring. This is also how you debug your own working.
steps.proof: They worked strictly left to right: 10 - 2 = 8, 8 x 3 = 24, 24 + 4 = 28. The correct answer is 8.
steps.pitfall: Fixing the final number without finding the step that produced it, so the same slip returns.

problems.prompt: Someone evaluated 10 - 2 x 3 as 24. Name the mistake.
problems.answer: They subtracted before multiplying; the answer is 4.

problems.prompt: A student gets 28 from 10 - 2 x 3 + 4. Name the order they used and give the right answer.
problems.answer: Strictly left to right. The correct answer is 8.

problems.prompt: A student writes 24 / 2 x 3 = 4. Give the correct value and the rule they broke.
problems.answer: 36. Division and multiplication rank equally and settle left to right.

steps.title: Polynomial Behaviour
steps.mastery: Predict the shape and end behaviour of a polynomial from its leading term.
steps.practice: Say what y = -2x^3 + 5x does as x goes to plus and minus infinity, and give its maximum number of roots.
steps.detail: The highest power dominates once x is large, so it alone fixes both ends. Odd degree means the ends go opposite ways; a negative leading coefficient flips them. Degree caps the number of roots and the number of turning points at one less.
steps.proof: Down on the right, up on the left, and at most 3 roots.
steps.pitfall: Reading the end behaviour off the constant term rather than the leading one.

steps.title: Rational Functions
steps.mastery: Locate the asymptotes and holes of a rational function.
steps.practice: Find every asymptote and hole of y = (x^2 - 4)/(x^2 - x - 2).
steps.detail: Factor both parts first. A factor cancelling top and bottom is a hole; one left in the denominator is a vertical asymptote. The horizontal behaviour comes from comparing degrees — equal degrees give the ratio of leading coefficients.
steps.proof: A hole at x = 2, a vertical asymptote at x = -1, and y = 1 horizontally.
steps.pitfall: Calling every zero of the denominator an asymptote, when a shared factor gives a hole.

steps.title: Exponentials and Logs Together
steps.mastery: Move between exponential and logarithmic form and solve either.
steps.practice: Solve 2^(x+1) = 40 to three decimal places, then solve log base 5 of (x - 1) = 2.
steps.detail: Logs undo exponentials. Take logs of both sides to bring a variable exponent down; exponentiate to undo a log. Any log equation needs its answer checked against the domain, because the algebra will happily return a value that makes the argument negative.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting to check the log solution lies in the domain of the original expression.

steps.title: Trig Identities
steps.mastery: Simplify or verify an expression using the standard identities.
steps.practice: Verify that (1 - cos^2 x)/sin x equals sin x for every x where it is defined.
steps.detail: Start from the messier side and transform it into the other, one identity per line, naming the identity used. The Pythagorean identity does most of the work. Note the excluded values — the two sides agree only where the original is defined.
steps.proof: 1 - cos^2 x is sin^2 x, so the fraction is sin^2 x over sin x.
steps.pitfall: Working on both sides at once, which proves the two are consistent rather than equal.

steps.title: Solve Trig Equations in Range
steps.mastery: Find every solution of a trig equation in a stated interval.
steps.practice: Solve 2 cos x - 1 = 0 for x between 0 and 360 degrees.
steps.detail: Isolate the ratio, take the inverse for the first solution, then use the symmetry of the circle for the rest in range. Cosine is positive in the first and fourth quadrants, so a positive cosine has two answers in a full turn.
steps.pitfall: Reporting the single value the calculator gives and missing the reflection.

steps.title: Transform Any Function
steps.mastery: Describe and apply shifts, stretches and reflections to any graph.
steps.practice: Describe how y = -3f(x - 2) + 1 differs from y = f(x), in the order the changes apply.
steps.detail: Inside the bracket acts on the input and runs backwards; outside acts on the output and runs forwards. Order matters: stretch and reflect before translating vertically. Track one point through every stage as a check.
steps.proof: Right 2, vertical stretch by 3, reflected in the x-axis, then up 1.
steps.pitfall: Applying the vertical shift before the reflection, which moves it the wrong way.

steps.title: Functions in Pieces
steps.mastery: Evaluate and sketch a piecewise function, including at its joins.
steps.practice: For f(x) = x^2 when x < 2 and 3x - 2 otherwise, find f(1), f(2) and f(3), and say whether it is continuous at 2.
steps.detail: Check which condition the input satisfies before substituting; only one branch applies. At a join, evaluate the limit from each side — equal means continuous, different means a jump. Draw open and closed circles on the sketch to show which piece owns the endpoint.
steps.proof: 1, 4 and 7; continuous, because both pieces approach 4.
steps.pitfall: Using the wrong branch at the boundary, where the inequality decides which applies.

steps.title: Ready for Limits
steps.mastery: Evaluate an expression that is undefined at a point by simplifying first.
steps.practice: Simplify (x^2 - 9)/(x - 3) and say what it approaches as x nears 3.
steps.detail: Factor and cancel to remove the problem factor. The simplified form agrees with the original everywhere except the removed point, which is exactly the distinction a limit is built on: what a function approaches need not be what it equals.
steps.proof: It equals x + 3 everywhere except x = 3, and approaches 6.
steps.pitfall: Concluding that the expression equals 6 at x = 3, where it is undefined.

steps.title: Probability as a Fraction
steps.mastery: Express a probability as favourable outcomes over total outcomes.
steps.practice: Find the probability of drawing a heart from a standard 52-card deck, and of drawing a face card.
steps.detail: Count the whole sample space first and write it down, then count what counts as success. Every probability lands between 0 and 1, so a result outside that is an arithmetic error rather than a surprising finding.
steps.pitfall: Counting the favourable outcomes correctly and the total wrongly.

steps.title: Not This
steps.mastery: Use the complement to get a probability that is awkward head-on.
steps.practice: Find the probability of at least one head in 3 fair coin tosses.
steps.detail: P(at least one) is 1 - P(none). Counting directly means splitting into exactly one, exactly two and exactly three and adding, which is three chances to slip. The complement is one line.
steps.proof: 7/8, from 1 minus the 1/8 chance of no heads at all.
steps.pitfall: Adding the three single-head probabilities and passing 1.

steps.title: And, Or, and Overlap
steps.mastery: Combine two events correctly depending on whether they can both happen.
steps.practice: From one card, find P(heart or face card).
steps.detail: For 'or', add and subtract the overlap. For 'and' with independent events, multiply. The word that decides it is whether the two can occur together — mutually exclusive events have no overlap to subtract.
steps.proof: 22/52 = 11/26, from 13 + 12 - 3 face cards that are hearts.
steps.pitfall: Adding 13/52 and 12/52 and double-counting the three hearts that are face cards.

steps.title: With and Without Replacement
steps.mastery: Adjust the second probability when the first draw changes the pool.
steps.practice: From 5 red and 3 blue counters, find P(two reds) with replacement and without.
steps.detail: With replacement the pool resets and the two draws are independent. Without, both numerator and denominator drop by one for the colour taken. Write the second fraction out fully rather than reusing the first.
steps.proof: 25/64 with, and 5/14 without.
steps.pitfall: Leaving the denominator at 8 on the second draw after removing a counter.

steps.title: Tree Diagrams
steps.mastery: Lay out a two-stage experiment as a tree and read probabilities off it.
steps.practice: Draw the tree for taking 2 sweets from a bag of 4 toffees and 6 mints, then find P(one of each).
steps.detail: Multiply along a branch, add across branches. Every set of branches leaving a node must total 1, which is the check that catches a mislabelled tree before you use it. A mixed outcome needs both orders added, not one.
steps.proof: 8/15, from the two mixed branches at 4/15 each.
steps.pitfall: Finding one mixed branch and forgetting the other order.

steps.title: Conditional Probability
steps.mastery: Compute the probability of one event given that another has occurred.
steps.practice: Of 30 students, 18 play football and 7 of those also play chess. Find P(chess given football).
steps.detail: Given narrows the sample space. P(A given B) is P(A and B) over P(B), and the denominator is the condition rather than the total. Re-read which event is the condition — swapping them gives a different and usually very different answer.
steps.pitfall: Dividing by the whole 30 rather than by the 18 the condition restricts you to.

steps.title: Where Intuition Fails
steps.mastery: Work through a probability result that contradicts the obvious answer.
steps.practice: For the Monty Hall problem with 3 doors, compute the win probability for switching and for staying.
steps.detail: The host's choice is not random — he never opens the car — so opening a door carries information. Enumerate the three equally likely initial picks and follow each through. Writing out all three cases is what converts disbelief into agreement.
steps.proof: 2/3 for switching and 1/3 for staying.
steps.pitfall: Assuming the two remaining doors are equally likely once one is opened.

steps.title: Expected Value
steps.mastery: Compute the long-run average outcome of a chance process.
steps.practice: A game pays 10 on a six and costs 2 to play. Find the expected value per game with a fair die.
steps.detail: Multiply each outcome by its probability and add. The result is an average over many plays and need not be a value the game can actually pay. A negative expected value means the game loses money in the long run however good one night looks.
steps.proof: -1/3: the payout averages 10/6, minus the 2 stake.
steps.pitfall: Comparing the prize with the stake and ignoring how rarely the prize lands.

steps.title: Claim, Reason, Conclusion
steps.mastery: Tell a proof apart from a demonstration of particular cases.
steps.practice: Say why checking that 3, 5 and 7 are odd primes does not prove every odd number above 1 is prime.
steps.detail: A proof argues from things already agreed to the claim, with a reason at every step. Examples can only ever disprove: one counterexample kills a universal claim, and a thousand confirmations do not establish it. Hunt for the counterexample before trying to prove anything.
steps.proof: 9 is odd and not prime, so three examples establish nothing about all cases.
steps.pitfall: Treating a run of confirming examples as evidence that a claim holds generally.

steps.title: Direct Proof
steps.mastery: Prove a claim by arguing straight from the definitions.
steps.practice: Prove that the sum of any two even numbers is even, writing them as 2m and 2n.
steps.detail: Write each object in its defining form with its own letter — 2m and 2n, not 2n twice. Manipulate until the conclusion's defining form appears. State which definition you used at the start and which you arrived at.
steps.proof: 2m + 2n = 2(m + n), which is 2 times an integer and so even.
steps.pitfall: Writing the two evens as 2n and 2n, which proves it only when they are equal.

steps.title: Find a Counterexample
steps.mastery: Disprove a universal claim by producing one case that breaks it.
steps.practice: Disprove: every number of the form n^2 + n + 41 is prime.
steps.detail: One case is enough, and it must be a genuine instance of the claim rather than an edge case the claim excluded. Try the boundaries first: zero, one, negatives, and the value that makes a term vanish or repeat.
steps.proof: n = 41 gives 41 x 43, which is not prime.
steps.pitfall: Testing only small n, where this particular claim holds for the first forty values.

steps.title: Proof by Contradiction
steps.mastery: Prove a claim by assuming its negation and deriving an impossibility.
steps.practice: Prove that the square root of 2 is irrational.
steps.detail: Assume the opposite, reason correctly, and arrive at a statement that cannot be true. The contradiction must be flat — a thing both true and false — not just unexpected. State the assumption explicitly at the top so the reader knows what is being discharged.
steps.proof: Assuming it is p/q in lowest terms forces both p and q even, contradicting lowest terms.
steps.pitfall: Deriving something merely surprising and calling it a contradiction.

steps.title: Proof by Induction
steps.mastery: Prove a statement for all integers from a base case and a step.
steps.practice: Prove that 2^n > n for every positive integer n.
steps.detail: Base case, assumption at k, then the claim at k+1 derived from that assumption. Write the assumption as an inequality or equation you can substitute. If the step would work without it, the proof is wrong somewhere.
steps.proof: n = 1 gives 2 > 1; and if 2^k > k then 2^(k+1) = 2 x 2^k > 2k >= k+1.
steps.pitfall: Never actually using the assumption in the inductive step, which proves nothing.

steps.title: Construction and Existence
steps.mastery: Prove something exists by producing one, and read a non-constructive proof.
steps.practice: Prove that there are infinitely many primes, using Euclid's argument.
steps.detail: An existence claim can be settled by exhibiting an example. Euclid's argument is subtler: it shows any finite list is incomplete without naming the missing prime. Note what it does and does not produce — that distinction is the whole interest of it.
steps.proof: Any finite list multiplied together plus 1 has a prime factor on no such list.
steps.pitfall: Claiming the new number is itself prime, which it need not be.

steps.title: Find the Broken Step
steps.mastery: Locate the invalid line in an argument that reaches a false conclusion.
steps.practice: An argument divides by (a - b) after setting a = b, and concludes 1 = 2. Name the invalid step.
steps.detail: Work down the argument and test each line for the operation it performs and whether that operation is always allowed. Division by a quantity that could be zero, taking a square root and keeping one sign, and squaring both sides all hide here.
steps.proof: Dividing by a - b is dividing by zero, which is not a permitted operation.
steps.pitfall: Rejecting the conclusion without being able to say which line failed.

steps.title: Write One Up
steps.mastery: Present a proof another person can follow and check line by line.
steps.practice: Write a full proof that (2m+1)(2n+1) is odd, with a reason on every line.
steps.detail: Say what you are proving, what you assume, then each step with its reason, then the conclusion. Read it back as somebody who does not already believe it. A proof only you can follow has not done its job.
steps.proof: (2m+1)(2n+1) = 2(2mn + m + n) + 1, which is odd by definition.
steps.pitfall: Leaving the algebra to speak for itself, so the reader has to reconstruct the reasoning.

steps.title: Recognise a Quadratic
steps.mastery: Identify whether an expression or equation is quadratic, and name a, b and c.
steps.practice: Say which of 3x^2 - 7x + 2, x^3 + 1, 5x - 2 and 4 - 9x^2 are quadratic.
steps.detail: A quadratic has a highest power of exactly 2 in one variable. Rewrite each one in the form ax^2 + bx + c before deciding, filling in zeros where a term is absent. For 4 - 9x^2 that is -9x^2 + 0x + 4, so a is -9, b is 0 and c is 4.
steps.proof: The first and the last; the second is cubic and the third is linear.
steps.pitfall: Missing a quadratic written out of order, such as 4 - 9x^2, because it does not open with the squared term.

problems.prompt: Is 5x - 2 quadratic?
problems.answer: No. Its highest power of x is 1, so it is linear.

problems.prompt: For 4 - 9x^2, write it as ax^2 + bx + c and give a, b and c.
Say which of 3x^2 - 7x + 2, x^3 + 1, 5x - 2 and 4 - 9x^2 are quadratic, and name the degree of each.
problems.answer: The first and last are quadratic (degree 2); x^3 + 1 is degree 3 and 5x - 2 is degree 1.

steps.title: Expand Binomials
steps.mastery: Expand a product of two brackets accurately, collecting the middle terms.
steps.practice: Expand (2x - 3)(x + 7), then expand (x + 5)^2.
steps.detail: Multiply each term in the first bracket by each term in the second — four products for two binomials. The two middle products combine into a single term. A squared bracket is still two brackets, so it still has four products and a middle term of twice the cross product.
steps.pitfall: Writing (x + 5)^2 as x^2 + 25, which drops the two middle terms entirely.

problems.prompt: Expand (x + 2)(x + 5).
Expand (2x - 3)(x + 7).
problems.hint: The middle term is 14x - 3x.

problems.prompt: Expand (x + 5)^2 and say what is wrong with writing it as x^2 + 25.
problems.answer: x^2 + 10x + 25. Writing x^2 + 25 drops the two cross terms that make up 10x.

steps.title: Factor Simple Quadratics
steps.mastery: Reverse the expansion to factor x^2 + bx + c into two brackets.
steps.practice: Factor x^2 - 7x + 12, then factor x^2 + 2x - 15.
steps.detail: Find two numbers multiplying to c and adding to b. With c positive both share b's sign; with c negative they have opposite signs and the larger carries b's sign. List the factor pairs of c rather than guessing at them.
steps.proof: (x - 3)(x - 4), and (x + 5)(x - 3); expanding either returns the original.
steps.pitfall: Getting the signs wrong when c is positive but b is negative, so both factors must be negative.

problems.prompt: Factor x^2 + 5x + 6.
Factor x^2 - 7x + 12.
problems.hint: c is positive and b negative, so both numbers are negative.

problems.prompt: Factor x^2 + 2x - 15, then expand your answer to check it.
problems.answer: (x + 5)(x - 3), and expanding returns x^2 + 2x - 15.

steps.title: Factor With a Leading Coefficient
steps.mastery: Factor a quadratic whose squared term has a coefficient other than 1.
steps.practice: Factor 2x^2 + 7x + 3, then factor 6x^2 - x - 2.
steps.detail: Multiply a by c and find two numbers with that product which add to b. Split the middle term into those two, then factor in pairs. For 2x^2 + 7x + 3 the product is 6, the pair is 1 and 6, and the split gives 2x^2 + x + 6x + 3.
steps.pitfall: Ignoring the leading coefficient and factoring as though a were 1.

problems.prompt: Factor 2x^2 + 7x + 3.
Factor 6x^2 - x - 2.
problems.hint: a times c is -12; find two numbers with product -12 and sum -1.

problems.prompt: Factor 4x^2 - 12x + 9 and say what is special about the result.
problems.answer: (2x - 3)^2. It is a perfect square, so the quadratic has one repeated root.

steps.title: Complete the Square
steps.mastery: Rewrite a quadratic in the form (x + p)^2 + q and read its vertex off.
steps.practice: Write x^2 + 6x + 1 in completed-square form, then state the vertex of its parabola.
steps.detail: Halve the coefficient of x and square it. Add that number and immediately subtract it, so nothing changes. Here half of 6 is 3 and 3 squared is 9, giving x^2 + 6x + 9 - 9 + 1. The first three terms are (x + 3)^2 and the rest is -8.
steps.proof: (x + 3)^2 - 8, so the vertex is at (-3, -8).
steps.pitfall: Forgetting to subtract the square you added, which changes the expression rather than rewriting it.

problems.prompt: Complete the square on x^2 + 6x.
Write x^2 + 6x + 1 in completed-square form and state the vertex.
Write x^2 - 5x + 2 in completed-square form, keeping fractions exact.
problems.hint: Half of -5 is -5/2, and its square is 25/4.

steps.title: Use the Formula
steps.mastery: Solve any quadratic with the formula, and read the discriminant for the number of roots.
steps.practice: Solve 2x^2 - 4x - 3 = 0 using the quadratic formula, then state the discriminant of x^2 + x + 5.
steps.detail: Substitute with brackets around every coefficient, negatives included. Compute b^2 - 4ac first and on its own: positive gives two roots, zero gives one, negative gives none over the reals. The formula always works, which makes it the fallback rather than the first choice.
steps.proof: x = (2 + sqrt 10)/2 and (2 - sqrt 10)/2; the second discriminant is -19, so there are no real roots.
steps.pitfall: Dropping the minus sign on b, so -4 goes into the formula as 4.

problems.prompt: Give the discriminant of x^2 + x + 5 and say how many real roots it has.
problems.answer: -19, so no real roots.

problems.prompt: Solve 2x^2 - 4x - 3 = 0 with the quadratic formula, leaving a surd.
problems.answer: x = (2 + sqrt 10)/2 and (2 - sqrt 10)/2.
problems.hint: The discriminant is 16 + 24 = 40.

problems.prompt: Solve 3x^2 - 2x - 8 = 0 with the formula and check your roots by factoring.
problems.answer: x = 2 and x = -4/3, and the quadratic factors as (3x + 4)(x - 2).

steps.title: Pick the Quickest Route
steps.mastery: Choose between factoring, completing the square and the formula before starting.
steps.practice: For x^2 - 9x + 20 = 0, 3x^2 + 5x - 1 = 0 and x^2 + 4x - 6 = 0, name the best method for each and solve one.
steps.detail: Try factoring first and abandon it after about twenty seconds. Complete the square when the question wants a vertex or when a is 1 and b is even. Use the formula when nothing factors neatly. Spending ten seconds choosing saves more than it costs.
steps.proof: Factoring, the formula, and completing the square; x^2 - 9x + 20 factors to (x - 4)(x - 5).
steps.pitfall: Reaching for the formula every time, which turns a ten-second factorisation into two minutes of arithmetic.

problems.prompt: Solve x^2 - 9x + 20 = 0 by the quickest method.
problems.answer: Factoring gives (x - 4)(x - 5), so x = 4 and x = 5.

problems.prompt: For 3x^2 + 5x - 1 = 0, name the best method and say why the others are worse.
problems.answer: The formula: nothing factors neatly and a is not 1, so completing the square brings fractions.

problems.prompt: For x^2 + 4x - 6 = 0, name the best method, solve it, and give the vertex of the parabola.
problems.answer: Completing the square gives (x + 2)^2 - 10, so x = -2 +/- sqrt 10 and the vertex is (-2, -10).

steps.title: Spot the Rule
steps.mastery: Work out the rule generating a sequence and continue it.
steps.practice: Give the next two terms of 3, 7, 11, 15 and of 2, 6, 18, 54, and name each rule.
steps.detail: Check the differences first, then the ratios. A constant difference is arithmetic, a constant ratio geometric. Test your rule against every term given, not just the last two — many sequences agree for three terms and diverge on the fourth.
steps.proof: 19 and 23 by adding 4; 162 and 486 by multiplying by 3.
steps.pitfall: Assuming a sequence is arithmetic because the first two gaps happen to match.

steps.title: The nth Term
steps.mastery: Write a formula for the nth term of an arithmetic sequence.
steps.practice: Find the nth term of 5, 8, 11, 14, then use it to find the 50th term.
steps.detail: The coefficient of n is the common difference. Substitute n = 1 into that alone and compare with the real first term; the gap is the constant to add. Always test the formula on two known terms before using it on an unknown one.
steps.proof: 3n + 2, and the 50th term is 152.
steps.pitfall: Writing 3n and forgetting the constant that fixes the first term.

steps.title: Arithmetic Series
steps.mastery: Sum an arithmetic sequence without adding the terms one at a time.
steps.practice: Sum the first 100 whole numbers, then sum 5 + 8 + 11 + ... + 152.
steps.detail: Pair the first with the last: each pair totals the same, and there are n/2 pairs. So the sum is n times the average of the first and last terms. Count the terms with (last - first)/difference + 1, and check that count separately.
steps.proof: 5050, and 3925 over 50 terms.
steps.pitfall: Getting the number of terms wrong by one, which is the commonest error in the whole topic.

steps.title: Geometric Sequences
steps.mastery: Find terms and sums of a sequence with a constant ratio.
steps.practice: For 3, 6, 12, 24, find the 10th term and the sum of the first 10 terms.
steps.detail: The nth term is a times r to the power n-1, and the sum is a(r^n - 1)/(r - 1). Note the n-1: the first term has been multiplied by r zero times. Check the ratio is genuinely constant across every pair before using either formula.
steps.pitfall: Using the arithmetic sum formula on a geometric sequence.

steps.title: Infinite Sums
steps.mastery: Decide whether an infinite geometric series settles on a value, and find it.
steps.practice: Sum 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + ... , then say what happens to 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + ...
steps.detail: An infinite geometric series converges only when the ratio is strictly between -1 and 1, and then sums to a/(1 - r). Check the ratio before reaching for the formula — used outside that range it returns a confident and meaningless number.
steps.proof: The first sums to 2; the second grows without limit.
steps.pitfall: Applying the infinite-sum formula when the ratio is 1 or greater.

steps.title: Recursive Definitions
steps.mastery: Read and use a sequence defined in terms of its own earlier terms.
steps.practice: For a(1) = 2 and a(n) = 3a(n-1) - 1, compute the first five terms.
steps.detail: A recursive rule needs the previous term, so the terms come out in order and there is no shortcut to the hundredth. Tabulate n and a(n) in two columns and fill down. Some recursions have a closed form; most useful ones do not.
steps.pitfall: Substituting n into the rule as though it were a closed formula.

steps.title: Prove a Formula by Induction
steps.mastery: Prove a statement for all n by base case and inductive step.
steps.practice: Prove that 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n+1)/2 for every positive integer n.
steps.detail: Three parts, all required: check n = 1, assume it holds at n = k, then derive it at n = k+1 using that assumption. Write the assumption out as a line of algebra. A step that never uses it has proved nothing.
steps.proof: n = 1 gives 1; assuming it for k, adding k+1 gives (k+1)(k+2)/2, which is the formula at k+1.
steps.pitfall: Proving the base case and the step and never stating the assumption being used.

steps.title: Where Series Appear
steps.mastery: Recognise a sequence or series inside a problem not stated as one.
steps.practice: A loan of 1000 grows 5% a year with no repayments. Write the balance after n years and find n when it passes 2000.
steps.detail: Repeated proportional change is geometric; repeated fixed change is arithmetic. Decide which before writing anything. Compound interest, population growth and depreciation are all the same geometric sequence wearing different words.
steps.proof: 1000 x 1.05^n, which passes 2000 during year 15.
steps.pitfall: Adding 5% of the original each year, which is arithmetic rather than geometric.

steps.title: Three Averages
steps.mastery: Compute mean, median and mode, and say which one a dataset calls for.
steps.practice: For 3, 7, 7, 8, 40, find all three averages and say which best describes the set.
steps.detail: Mean is the total over the count, median the middle once ordered, mode the commonest. One extreme value moves the mean and leaves the median alone, which is why house prices are quoted as medians. Order the data first — an unordered median is the commonest slip.
steps.proof: Mean 13, median 7, mode 7; the median, because 40 drags the mean above every other value.
steps.pitfall: Quoting the mean on a skewed set, where it describes no member of it.

steps.title: Spread, Not Just Centre
steps.mastery: Measure how spread out a dataset is with range and interquartile range.
steps.practice: For 2, 4, 4, 5, 9, 12, 15, find the range and the interquartile range.
steps.detail: Range is max minus min and one outlier controls it. The IQR is the middle half — the upper quartile minus the lower — and ignores the tails, which is what makes it the honest one. Two sets can share a mean and share nothing else.
steps.proof: Range 13, IQR 8, from quartiles at 4 and 12.
steps.pitfall: Reporting a centre with no spread, so two very different sets look identical.

steps.title: Read a Chart Honestly
steps.mastery: Spot the ways a chart can mislead while being factually correct.
steps.practice: A bar chart of 98, 99 and 101 starts its axis at 97. Say what the reader will conclude and why it is wrong.
steps.detail: Check three things on any chart: where the axis starts, what the units are, and whether the scale is linear. A bar chart with a truncated axis is the commonest honest lie in print. Redraw it from zero and see how much of the effect survives.
steps.proof: The last bar looks four times the first; truncating the axis exaggerates a 3% difference.
steps.pitfall: Trusting the shape of a chart without reading the axis.

steps.title: Standard Deviation
steps.mastery: Compute a standard deviation and say what it means for the data.
steps.practice: Find the standard deviation of 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9.
steps.detail: Subtract the mean from each value, square the differences, average those, then take the square root. The squaring is what stops the positives and negatives cancelling. The result is in the same units as the data, which the variance is not, and that is why it is the one quoted.
steps.proof: 2, since the variance is 4.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting the final square root and reporting the variance instead.

steps.title: Correlation Is Not Cause
steps.mastery: Read a scatter plot for strength and direction without claiming a cause.
steps.practice: Ice cream sales and drowning rates correlate at 0.9. Give a third factor that explains both.
steps.detail: A correlation coefficient runs from -1 to 1 and measures how closely points follow a line. It says nothing about direction of influence. Before claiming a cause, ask what third thing could move both, and whether the relationship could run the other way.
steps.proof: Temperature. Hot weather raises both independently.
steps.pitfall: Reading a strong correlation as evidence that one variable drives the other.

steps.title: Sample and Bias
steps.mastery: Judge whether a sample can support the claim being made from it.
steps.practice: A website poll of its own readers reports 78% support. Name the bias and say who is missing.
steps.detail: Ask who could have been picked, who actually answered, and who was never in the frame. A biased sample of ten thousand is worse than a random sample of a hundred, because the size lends it false authority. Name the population the claim is about before judging the sample.
steps.proof: Self-selection: only readers who felt strongly, and only that site's audience, ever answered.
steps.pitfall: Treating a large sample as a representative one, when size does not fix bias.

steps.title: Say What the Data Cannot
steps.mastery: State the limits of a dataset alongside the conclusion drawn from it.
steps.practice: Take a claim like "our users are 40% faster" and write 2 sentences: what the data shows, and one question it cannot settle.
steps.detail: A conclusion without its limits is a conclusion somebody will over-apply. Name the population, the time window and the thing you did not measure. 'More research is needed' is not a limit; 'this says nothing about anyone under 18' is.
steps.proof: The second sentence names a specific unanswered question, such as which users, or over what period.
steps.pitfall: Adding a vague disclaimer that does not name any particular limit.

steps.title: The Three Ratios
steps.mastery: State sine, cosine and tangent as ratios of sides in a right triangle.
steps.practice: In a right triangle with opposite 3, adjacent 4 and hypotenuse 5, write sin, cos and tan of the angle.
steps.detail: Opposite and adjacent are named from the angle you are working with, and only the hypotenuse is fixed. Label the triangle from that angle every single time before writing a ratio. SOH CAH TOA is the mnemonic; the labelling is the skill.
steps.pitfall: Labelling opposite and adjacent relative to the right angle rather than to the angle in question.

steps.title: Find a Missing Side
steps.mastery: Use a trig ratio to find an unknown side given an angle and one side.
steps.practice: A right triangle has a 35 degree angle and a hypotenuse of 10. Find the side opposite that angle, to two decimal places.
steps.detail: Decide which two sides the question involves, pick the ratio that links them, then rearrange before substituting. Check the mode on the calculator once at the start of any trig session. A side longer than the hypotenuse is always an error.
steps.proof: 5.74, from 10 sin 35.
steps.pitfall: Leaving the calculator in radians, which gives 10 sin 35 as about -4.28.

steps.title: Find a Missing Angle
steps.mastery: Use an inverse trig function to recover an angle from two sides.
steps.practice: A right triangle has opposite 7 and adjacent 24. Find the angle to one decimal place.
steps.detail: Form the ratio from the two sides you have, then apply the inverse of the matching function. The answer must lie between 0 and 90 in a right triangle, which is the sanity check. Keep full precision until the final rounding.
steps.proof: 16.3 degrees, from arctan of 7/24.
steps.pitfall: Using the ratio rather than its inverse, and getting a number that is not an angle.

steps.title: Build the Unit Circle
steps.mastery: Read sine and cosine off the unit circle for the standard angles.
steps.practice: Give sin and cos of 0, 30, 45, 60 and 90 degrees without a table.
steps.detail: Cosine is the x coordinate of the point on the circle and sine is the y. Two triangles — 30-60-90 and 45-45-90 — generate every standard value, so draw those once and read the rest off them. Derived beats memorised because it comes back after a month away.
steps.proof: Sine runs 0, 1/2, root2/2, root3/2, 1; cosine runs the same values backwards.
steps.pitfall: Memorising the table and losing it, rather than deriving it from two triangles.

steps.title: Beyond the First Quadrant
steps.mastery: Determine the sign of each ratio in any quadrant and find related angles.
steps.practice: Give sin 150, cos 210 and tan 315 exactly, using the reference angle each time.
steps.detail: Find the reference angle to the nearest part of the x-axis, evaluate there, then attach the sign from the quadrant. Sketch the circle and mark the quadrant before answering — the value and the sign are two separate decisions and mixing them is the whole difficulty.
steps.pitfall: Taking the reference angle correctly and then forgetting the sign the quadrant demands.

steps.title: Trig as a Wave
steps.mastery: Sketch y = sin x and y = cos x and state period and amplitude.
steps.practice: Plot y = 2 sin x across a full turn, then give the height of its peak and the width of one cycle of y = sin 2x.
steps.detail: A multiplier outside stretches the graph vertically and sets the amplitude. A multiplier inside squeezes it horizontally and divides the period. Plot the five key points of one cycle rather than sketching a freehand wave.
steps.proof: The peak is at 2; one cycle of y = sin 2x spans 180 degrees.
steps.pitfall: Swapping the two effects, so the coefficient inside the function is read as the amplitude.

steps.title: Solve a Trig Equation
steps.mastery: Find every solution of a trig equation within a stated range.
steps.practice: Solve sin x = 0.5 for x between 0 and 360 degrees.
steps.detail: The inverse function returns one angle. Use the symmetry of the circle to find the others in range: for sine, the second is 180 minus the first. Sketch the wave and draw the horizontal line — the number of crossings is the number of answers you owe.
steps.pitfall: Giving only the calculator's answer and missing the second solution in range.

steps.title: Identify Net Force on a Box
steps.mastery: Determine the resultant force acting on an object by vector addition of all applied forces.
steps.practice: Calculate the net force on a 5 kg box pushed with 12 N east and pulled with 8 N west.
steps.detail: Place the box on a frictionless surface. Write each force as a signed number along the east‑west axis (east positive, west negative). Add the numbers to get the net force. Verify the sign tells you the direction. This step builds the habit of treating forces as vectors before using Newton's laws.
steps.proof: 12 N − 8 N = 4 N east, which is the correct vector sum.
steps.pitfall: Adding magnitudes without keeping track of direction, especially when forces oppose each other.

steps.title: Apply Newton's First Law
steps.mastery: Predict that an object with zero net force maintains its current state of motion.
steps.practice: State what happens to a 2 kg puck sliding at 3 m/s on a frictionless ice surface when no horizontal forces act on it.
steps.detail: Recall that the first law (inertia) says motion does not change without net force. Write the initial velocity vector, confirm that all horizontal forces sum to zero, and then state that the velocity remains unchanged for any amount of time. Use the result from step 1 to verify the net force is indeed zero.
steps.proof: The puck continues at 3 m/s in the same direction because the net force is zero.
steps.pitfall: Assuming the object will eventually stop even when friction is absent.

problems.prompt: A 1 kg puck slides at 2 m/s on a frictionless ice surface with no horizontal forces acting. What happens to its motion?
problems.answer: It continues at 2 m/s in the same direction.

problems.prompt: State what happens to a 2 kg puck sliding at 3 m/s on a frictionless ice surface when no horizontal forces act on it.
problems.answer: It continues at 3 m/s in the same direction.

problems.prompt: A 0.5 kg cart moves at 4 m/s on a frictionless track and then travels through a region with no forces for 5 s. What is its speed after this interval?
problems.answer: 4 m/s.
problems.hint: Use Newton's first law; speed is unchanged when net force is zero.

steps.title: Use Newton's Second Law for Acceleration
steps.mastery: Calculate an object's acceleration by dividing the net force by its mass (F = ma).
steps.practice: Find the acceleration of a 3 kg cart when a net horizontal force of 15 N acts on it.
steps.detail: Take the net force from step 1 (or any given value). Write the formula a = F/m, plug in the numbers, and solve for a. Double‑check that the force is in newtons and mass in kilograms so the result is in meters per second squared. Record the acceleration vector with the same direction as the net force.
steps.proof: a = F/m = 15 N / 3 kg = 5 m/s², which matches the calculation.
steps.pitfall: Confusing mass with weight or forgetting to keep units consistent.

problems.prompt: Find the acceleration of a 2 kg object acted on by a net force of 6 N east.
problems.answer: 3 m/s² east.

problems.prompt: Find the acceleration of a 3 kg cart when a net horizontal force of 15 N acts on it.
problems.answer: 5 m/s² in the direction of the force.

problems.prompt: A 10 kg sled is pulled with 25 N north and 15 N south. What is its acceleration?
problems.answer: 1 m/s² north.
problems.hint: Subtract opposing forces before applying F=ma.

steps.title: Demonstrate Newton's Third Law Pairs
steps.mastery: Identify action‑reaction force pairs and state that they act on different bodies.
steps.practice: When a 10 N hand pushes a wall, write the force the wall exerts on the hand.
steps.detail: Label the hand as object A and the wall as object B. The force from A on B is 10 N forward; the reaction is a 10 N force from B on A backward. Emphasize that the two forces never cancel because they act on different bodies. Sketch a free‑body diagram for each object to visualise the pair.
steps.proof: The wall exerts a 10 N force on the hand opposite to the hand’s push, satisfying the third law.
steps.pitfall: Applying the reaction force to the same object that experiences the action force.

problems.prompt: A hand pushes a wall with 5 N. What force does the wall exert on the hand?
problems.answer: 5 N opposite direction.

problems.prompt: A book rests on a table. The Earth exerts a 9.8 N downward force on the book. What force does the book exert on the Earth?
problems.answer: 9.8 N upward.

problems.prompt: A person of 70 kg pushes a 100 kg crate with a horizontal force of 120 N. State the reaction force and the object on which it acts.
problems.answer: 120 N opposite direction acting on the person.
problems.hint: Action‑reaction forces act on different bodies.

steps.title: Solve a Two‑Body Interaction Problem
steps.mastery: Combine all three Newtonian laws to predict motion of interacting objects without assistance.
steps.practice: Two ice skaters, each 60 kg, push off each other with a 30 N force for 2 s. Calculate each skater’s final speed.
steps.detail: Use the third law to note each skater experiences a 30 N force in opposite directions. Apply the second law via impulse: Δp = F·t, then Δv = Δp/m. Since initial speeds are zero, the final speed equals Δv. Verify that momentum is conserved (total momentum remains zero). Write the answer as 1 m/s east for skater 1 and 1 m/s west for skater 2.
steps.proof: Impulse = F·t = 30 N·2 s = 60 Ns; Δv = Impulse/m = 60 Ns / 60 kg = 1 m/s for each skater, moving in opposite directions.
steps.pitfall: Adding the forces together instead of treating them as separate action‑reaction pairs on each skater.

problems.prompt: Two 50 kg skaters push off each other with a 20 N force for 1 s. What is the final speed of each skater?
problems.answer: 0.4 m/s in opposite directions.

problems.prompt: Two 60 kg ice skaters push off each other with a 30 N force for 2 s. Calculate each skater’s final speed.
problems.answer: 1 m/s in opposite directions.

problems.prompt: Two astronauts, masses 80 kg and 120 kg, push apart with a force that increases linearly from 0 to 40 N over 3 s. Assuming the average force is 20 N, find the final speeds of each astronaut.
problems.answer: 0.75 m/s for the 80 kg astronaut and 0.5 m/s for the 120 kg astronaut, opposite directions.
problems.hint: Use the average force to compute impulse, then divide by each mass.

steps.title: Clear the Interruptions
steps.mastery: Remove the things that will break a long block before it starts.
steps.practice: List the 5 things most likely to interrupt a 90-minute block and remove or defer each one now.
steps.detail: Do this before the block, not during: a phone face-down within reach is still a decision you make 40 times. Deal with the 5 by removing them from the room, silencing them, or telling somebody you are unavailable until a stated time. Anything you cannot remove gets a written note saying when you will handle it.
steps.proof: All 5 are removed, silenced or deferred in writing before the block begins.
steps.pitfall: Starting the block with the intention of ignoring 2 of them, which spends the block resisting instead of working.

problems.prompt: You cannot remove 1 of your 5 interruptions before a 90-minute block. What do you do with it?
problems.answer: Write down when you will handle it, so it stops competing during the block.

problems.prompt: Is a silenced phone left on the desk during a 90-minute block removed or deferred?
problems.answer: Neither — it is still 1 decision made repeatedly, so it leaves the room.

problems.prompt: Why deal with all 5 before the block rather than as they arrive?
problems.answer: Each one handled mid-block costs the state the block exists to build.

steps.title: One Difficult Thing
steps.mastery: Commit a whole block to a single hard piece of work.
steps.practice: Name the 1 difficult task a 90-minute block will hold, in 1 sentence, before starting.
steps.detail: A block with 3 tasks in it becomes a block of switching, and hard material needs the time that switching eats. Write the single task on the page where you can see it. If it turns out to be 4 tasks, that is a planning result worth having, and the block still runs on the first of them.
steps.proof: 1 written task, and the block's output is work on that task alone.
steps.pitfall: Sliding into email or an easier topic at the first hard point, which is the exact moment the block is earning.

problems.prompt: Your 90-minute block lists 3 tasks. What happens to the other 2?
problems.answer: They move out — the block runs on 1 task, and the others are scheduled separately.

problems.prompt: You hit a hard point 25 minutes in and want to switch to an easier topic. What is the instruction?
problems.answer: Stay — that point is where the block is doing its work.

problems.prompt: Why does hard material need a 90-minute block rather than 3 blocks of 30?
problems.answer: Getting back into difficult work costs time that short blocks spend repeatedly.

steps.title: Work in Timed Blocks
steps.mastery: Run a fixed block and stop when it ends rather than when you flag.
steps.practice: Run 2 blocks of 45 minutes with 1 break of 10, and record the finish time of each.
steps.detail: A fixed end makes the difficulty bearable and stops the block drifting into an hour of low-quality sitting. Set a timer out of sight. When it goes, stop mid-sentence if necessary, because stopping mid-thought makes the restart easier than stopping at a tidy boundary.
steps.proof: 2 recorded finish times, and the break taken between them was 10 minutes rather than 25.
steps.pitfall: Running 1 long block of 2 hours, where the last 40 minutes are sitting rather than working.

problems.prompt: You plan 2 blocks of 45 with a 10-minute break. What is the total elapsed time?
problems.answer: 100 minutes.

problems.prompt: The timer goes mid-sentence. Finish the paragraph or stop?
problems.answer: Stop — an unfinished thought makes the next restart faster.

problems.prompt: Why is 1 block of 120 minutes usually worse than 2 of 45?
problems.answer: The tail of a long block is sitting rather than working, and it pushes out the break that would restore attention.

steps.title: Keep a Distraction Sheet
steps.mastery: Park an intruding thought in writing instead of acting on it.
steps.practice: Keep 1 sheet beside you for a 45-minute block and write down each intruding thought in under 5 words.
steps.detail: The thought arrives whether you want it or not; the choice is whether you leave the work. Five words is enough to release it — "check train times" — and the sheet gets dealt with in the break. Count the entries: a block with 14 of them is telling you something about what needs sorting out before the next one.
steps.proof: A sheet of parked thoughts, none of which were acted on during the block.
steps.pitfall: Handling the small ones because they take 30 seconds, which is 30 seconds plus the way back.

problems.prompt: A thought arrives that would take 30 seconds to handle. Handle it or park it?
problems.answer: Park it — the cost is the 30 seconds plus getting back into the work.

problems.prompt: Your sheet holds 14 entries after 45 minutes. What does that number say?
problems.answer: That something outside the work needs sorting out before the next block.

problems.prompt: Why a 5-word limit on each entry?
problems.answer: Enough to let the thought go, short enough not to become the work.

steps.title: Mark Where You Stopped
steps.mastery: Leave a block with a note that makes the next one start fast.
steps.practice: End 1 block by writing 3 lines: where you stopped, what you were about to try, and the first action next time.
steps.detail: The expensive part of a block is the first 10 minutes, and this is what removes them. Write it while the work is still in your head — a note written the next morning is a guess. "Stuck on the sign in line 4; next try the substitution u = x - 1" is worth more than a page of summary.
steps.proof: 3 lines, ending with a named first action for the next block.
steps.pitfall: Writing "carry on where I left off", which is the note you will not be able to use.

problems.prompt: Which hand-off is usable: (a) "continue chapter 4", (b) "stuck on the sign in line 4; next try u = x - 1"?
problems.answer: (b). It names the exact next action.

problems.prompt: Why write the 3 lines at the end of the block rather than at the start of the next one?
problems.answer: The detail is still in your head; a day later it is reconstruction.

problems.prompt: What does a good hand-off save at the start of the next 45-minute block?
problems.answer: The first 10 minutes otherwise spent working out where you were.

steps.title: Protect the Same Hours
steps.mastery: Run deep blocks at a fixed time so they stop needing a decision.
steps.practice: Fix 2 deep blocks in the same 2 slots every week and defend them for 3 weeks.
steps.detail: A block scheduled by mood happens about half as often as one that is simply when you work. Pick 2 slots that are realistically yours, and treat everything else as negotiable around them. Record kept or missed for 3 weeks: below 4 out of 6, the slots are wrong rather than your discipline.
steps.proof: A 3-week record of the 2 weekly slots, marked kept or missed.
steps.pitfall: Choosing 2 slots you wish were free, which produces a record of misses and nothing else.

problems.prompt: Over 3 weeks you keep 3 of 6 fixed blocks. Is the problem the slots or the discipline?
problems.answer: The slots — below 4 of 6 usually means they were never realistically free.

problems.prompt: Why does a fixed weekly slot beat deciding each of the 7 days when to work?
problems.answer: It removes the decision, and a block left to mood happens roughly half as often.

problems.prompt: What are the 2 numbers this step asks you to record?
problems.answer: Blocks kept and blocks missed, over 3 weeks.

steps.title: Build Up the Length
steps.mastery: Extend block length gradually rather than attempting 3 hours cold.
steps.practice: Add 10 minutes a week to your longest block, starting from 45 and stopping at 90.
steps.detail: Long concentration is trained, not decided: an untrained 3-hour attempt produces 40 good minutes and the belief that you cannot do it. Add 10 minutes only after a full week of the current length held. If a week breaks down, repeat it rather than adding.
steps.proof: A weekly record showing 45, 55, 65 and so on, with each length held before the next was added.
steps.pitfall: Jumping from 45 to 120 in 1 week, which fails and teaches the wrong lesson.

problems.prompt: Starting at 45 minutes and adding 10 a week, how long until you reach 85?
problems.answer: 4 weeks.

problems.prompt: A week at 65 minutes breaks down twice. Add 10 or repeat 65?
problems.answer: Repeat 65 until the week holds.

problems.prompt: Why does an untrained 3-hour attempt teach the wrong lesson?
problems.answer: It produces about 40 useful minutes and the conclusion that long blocks are impossible.

steps.title: Judge the Block by Output
steps.mastery: Score a block on what it produced rather than how long it lasted.
steps.practice: Write 1 line of output for each of 3 blocks — problems solved, pages drafted, derivation finished — and compare.
steps.detail: Time at the desk is the input and is easy to mistake for the result. Recording output makes a 90-minute block that produced 2 solved problems visible next to a 45-minute one that produced 6. Where the long blocks produce less, the problem is usually the interruption sheet or the time of day.
steps.proof: 3 blocks with their outputs written down and compared.
steps.pitfall: Recording hours studied, which rewards sitting still.

problems.prompt: Block A ran 90 minutes and solved 2 problems; block B ran 45 and solved 6. Which was the better block?
problems.answer: B — the output is 3 times the rate.

problems.prompt: Why record output rather than the 90 minutes spent at the desk?
problems.answer: Hours reward sitting still; output shows whether the block worked.

problems.prompt: Your 90-minute blocks consistently produce less per minute than your 45s. Name 2 likely causes.
problems.answer: Interruptions during the long block, or running it at the wrong time of day.

steps.title: Read the Question Twice
steps.mastery: Establish what a question asks before writing anything.
steps.practice: Take 5 exam questions and underline the command word and the 2 constraints in each.
steps.detail: Command words are instructions: describe, explain, evaluate and calculate want different answers, and answering the wrong one scores near zero however good the content. Underline the command word, then the constraints — a date range, a named case, a unit — before any working starts.
steps.proof: 5 questions with the command word and constraints underlined.
steps.pitfall: Starting to write at the first familiar noun in the question, which is how a good answer to the wrong question happens.

problems.prompt: What is the difference between "describe" and "explain" in a 6-mark question?
problems.answer: Describe wants what happens; explain wants why it happens.

problems.prompt: A question says "evaluate, with reference to 2 examples". Name the 2 things that must appear.
problems.answer: A judgement, and 2 named examples supporting it.

problems.prompt: Why underline the 2 constraints before starting the working?
problems.answer: A correct answer outside the stated constraints scores little or nothing.

steps.title: Allocate Time by Marks
steps.mastery: Spend time on a question in proportion to what it is worth.
steps.practice: For a 90-minute paper worth 75 marks, work out the minutes per mark and the time for a 12-mark question.
steps.detail: Divide time by marks to get the rate, then multiply per question — and leave 10 per cent for reading and checking. Write the finish time beside each question on the paper before starting, so falling behind is visible at question 3 rather than at question 8.
steps.proof: A rate in minutes per mark and a written finish time beside each question.
steps.pitfall: Spending 25 minutes on a 4-mark question because it is interesting, which costs a whole later question.

problems.prompt: A 90-minute paper carries 75 marks. What is the rate in minutes per mark?
problems.answer: 1.2 minutes per mark.

problems.prompt: At 1.2 minutes per mark, how long does a 12-mark question get?
problems.answer: About 14 minutes.

problems.prompt: Why write finish times on the paper before starting question 1?
problems.answer: Falling behind becomes visible early, while there is still time to correct it.

steps.title: Answer What Is Asked
steps.mastery: Keep an answer inside the question rather than writing everything known.
steps.practice: Take 1 answer you wrote and cross out every sentence that the question did not ask for.
steps.detail: Extra content earns nothing and costs the time a later question needed. Read your answer against the command word and constraints: anything outside them goes. If half the answer disappears, that is time you can move to the questions you did not finish.
steps.proof: 1 marked-up answer where the crossings-out are all outside the question.
steps.pitfall: Writing everything you know on the topic in the hope that some of it earns credit.

problems.prompt: A 4-mark question gets 12 sentences from you. What is likely true?
problems.answer: Most of it is outside what was asked, and the time belonged to another question.

problems.prompt: Does extra correct content beyond a 4-mark question earn marks?
problems.answer: No — it earns nothing and costs time.

problems.prompt: You cross out half of 1 answer. What do you do with the time that represents?
problems.answer: Move it to the questions you did not finish.

steps.title: Show the Working
steps.mastery: Write the intermediate steps that method marks are given for.
steps.practice: Redo 3 problems writing every intermediate line, and count the marks a scheme would give for method alone.
steps.detail: A correct answer with no working scores the answer mark and loses the method ones; a wrong answer with full working keeps most of them. Write the formula, the substitution and the rearrangement as separate lines. This also makes a slip findable, which a page of mental arithmetic never is.
steps.proof: 3 problems with every line written, and a count of the method marks available.
steps.pitfall: Doing 2 steps in your head to save time, which loses both the marks and the chance to find the error.

problems.prompt: A wrong final answer with full working on a 5-mark question. Roughly what is kept?
problems.answer: Most of the method marks — often 3 or 4 of the 5.

problems.prompt: A right answer with no working on a 5-mark question. What is lost?
problems.answer: The method marks, keeping only the accuracy mark.

problems.prompt: Name the 3 lines worth writing separately in a calculation.
problems.answer: The formula, the substitution, and the rearrangement.

steps.title: Attempt Every Question
steps.mastery: Leave nothing blank, including what you cannot finish.
steps.practice: On a past paper, write at least 2 lines on every question including the 3 you cannot do.
steps.detail: A blank scores 0 with certainty; a stated formula and an attempt at substitution often scores 1 or 2. Go through at the end and put something on every blank — the definition, the relevant equation, or the first step. On a 75-mark paper this is routinely worth 5 marks.
steps.proof: No blank questions on the paper, and a count of marks the partial attempts earned.
steps.pitfall: Leaving the last question blank because time ran out, when 90 seconds of formula and substitution was available.

problems.prompt: 3 blanks on a paper, each worth 5 marks. What is the certain score for them?
What can 90 seconds on an unfinished question usually earn?
problems.answer: 1 or 2 method marks for the formula and a substitution.

problems.prompt: When in a 90-minute paper do you fill the blanks?
problems.answer: At the end, after every question you can do is done.

steps.title: Check in the Last Ten
steps.mastery: Use reserved time to check rather than to keep writing.
steps.practice: Reserve the last 10 minutes of a 90-minute paper and use them on units, signs and unanswered parts.
steps.detail: Check in a fixed order so nothing is missed: unanswered parts first, then final answers for units, then signs and magnitudes. Rereading prose for style is the least valuable use of the 10 minutes and the most tempting. Mark each question as checked so the pass is trackable.
steps.proof: A paper with every question marked checked, and the 3 kinds of error looked for.
steps.pitfall: Using the last 10 minutes to extend an answer that was already complete.

problems.prompt: In what order do you use the reserved 10 minutes?
problems.answer: Unanswered parts, then units on final answers, then signs and magnitudes.

problems.prompt: Is extending a complete 8-mark answer a good use of the last 10 minutes?
problems.answer: No — unanswered parts and unit checks are worth more.

problems.prompt: Why mark each question as checked during the 10-minute pass?
problems.answer: So the pass is trackable and no question is checked twice while another is missed.

steps.title: Plan the Long Answer
steps.mastery: Sketch the structure of an extended answer before writing it.
steps.practice: Plan a 16-mark essay answer in 4 bullet points and 1 line naming your conclusion, in 3 minutes.
steps.detail: Three minutes of planning buys a structure the marker can follow and stops the answer arriving at a conclusion it never argued for. Four bullets and a stated conclusion is enough; the plan is not marked, so it is written in note form and crossed out at the end if the paper asks.
steps.proof: 4 bullets and a named conclusion, written in 3 minutes before the answer.
steps.pitfall: Planning for 10 of the 20 minutes, which leaves an excellent plan and half an answer.

problems.prompt: A 16-mark answer has about 20 minutes. How long does the plan get?
problems.answer: About 3 minutes.

problems.prompt: What does the plan contain besides the 4 bullets?
problems.answer: One line naming the conclusion the answer will reach.

problems.prompt: Why does an unplanned 16-mark answer often reach an unargued conclusion?
problems.answer: The structure is being invented while writing, so the ending does not follow from the middle.

steps.title: Debrief the Paper
steps.mastery: Convert a completed paper into a list of specific fixes.
steps.practice: After marking a paper, write 3 fixes naming the question, the loss and the change.
steps.detail: "Do better on trigonometry" is not a fix. "Question 6: lost 3 marks for no units on final answers — add a unit check to the last 10 minutes" is. Three is enough to actually carry into the next paper, and they get checked against that paper's debrief.
steps.proof: 3 fixes, each naming a question, a loss and a change.
steps.pitfall: Writing a list of 12 fixes, none of which gets carried into the next paper.

problems.prompt: Turn "lost 3 marks on units" into a fix.
problems.answer: Add a unit check on every final answer to the reserved 10 minutes.

problems.prompt: Why cap the list at 3 fixes rather than 12?
problems.answer: 3 can be carried into the next paper; 12 cannot.

problems.prompt: What are the 3 parts of a usable fix?
problems.answer: The question, the loss, and the change to make.

steps.title: Explain to an Empty Room
steps.mastery: Deliver a topic aloud to nobody and hear where the explanation stops.
steps.practice: Explain 1 topic aloud for 3 minutes with the notes shut, and mark the 2 places you stalled.
steps.detail: Say it out loud rather than in your head — the head skips the joins and the mouth cannot. Stand up if it helps. When you stall, do not fix it yet: note where it happened and carry on to the end, because the second stall is often caused by the first.
steps.proof: You spoke for 3 minutes and can name the 2 points where the explanation broke down.
steps.pitfall: Explaining it silently, which skips exactly the joins that speaking exposes.

problems.prompt: Why does explaining aloud find gaps that explaining in your head does not, in under 20 words?
problems.answer: Speech has to supply the joins between ideas; silent thought skips them.

problems.prompt: You stall twice in a 3-minute explanation. Fix the first stall immediately or finish first?
problems.answer: Finish first — the second stall is often caused by the first.

problems.prompt: Which is the better record of the attempt: (a) "went badly", (b) 2 marked points where it stalled?
problems.answer: (b). Named stalls are 2 things to study; a feeling is none.

steps.title: Explain It to a Beginner
steps.mastery: Pitch an explanation at somebody who has none of the vocabulary.
steps.practice: Explain diffusion to a 10-year-old in 5 sentences, using no word they would have to look up.
steps.detail: Banning the vocabulary is the point: the terms are where understanding hides, because a sentence built from 3 technical words can be produced without meaning anything. Replace each term with what it does. If you cannot, that term is the thing to go and learn.
steps.proof: 5 sentences that a 10-year-old could follow, with no term left unexplained.
steps.pitfall: Keeping 1 technical word because there is no short substitute, which is the word you least understand.

problems.prompt: Explain "equilibrium" to a beginner in 1 sentence with no technical words.
problems.answer: Two things push against each other equally, so nothing moves overall.

problems.prompt: You cannot explain "entropy" without using "disorder" or "thermodynamic". What does that tell you?
problems.answer: That the term is being used as a label rather than understood, and it is the next thing to study.

problems.prompt: Which explanation is pitched right for a 10-year-old: (a) "osmosis is water moving down a potential gradient", (b) "water moves to where there is less water"?
problems.answer: (b). The first needs 2 terms explained before it means anything.

steps.title: Answer the Why Question
steps.mastery: Say why a result follows, not only what the result is.
steps.practice: State why dividing by a fraction multiplies by its reciprocal, in 3 sentences with 1 worked example.
steps.detail: The what is usually memorised and the why usually is not, so this is where an explanation breaks. Build from something you already accept — here, that dividing by 2 halves a quantity — and show the rule falling out of it. Finish with 1 example where the rule does the work.
steps.proof: Somebody who accepted your first sentence would have to accept the rule by the third.
steps.pitfall: Restating the rule in different words and calling it the reason.

problems.prompt: Why does 6 divided by 1/2 equal 12?
problems.answer: Because it asks how many halves fit in 6, and 12 halves do.

problems.prompt: Which is a why: (a) "invert and multiply", (b) "dividing asks how many of the divisor fit, and halves fit twice as often as wholes"?
problems.answer: (b). The first is the rule restated.

problems.prompt: State the 1 thing a why-explanation must start from.
problems.answer: Something the listener already accepts, so the result can be built rather than asserted.

steps.title: Take the Hard Question
steps.mastery: Field a question you did not prepare and locate the gap it exposes.
steps.practice: Give somebody your 5-sentence explanation and have them ask 3 questions you did not plan for.
steps.detail: A prepared explanation is a rehearsed path, and questions are what take you off it. Write each question down as it is asked rather than answering immediately — the ones you cannot answer are worth more than the ones you can, and they will be forgotten within a minute if unrecorded.
steps.proof: 3 written questions, marked answered or not.
steps.pitfall: Answering a question you half-know with confidence, which loses the gap it was pointing at.

problems.prompt: Of 3 unplanned questions you answer 2. Which is worth the most study time?
problems.answer: The 1 you could not answer.

problems.prompt: Why write a question down before answering it, in under 15 words?
problems.answer: An unrecorded gap is forgotten within a minute of the conversation moving on.

problems.prompt: Which is the better session: (a) 6 questions you all answered, (b) 3 questions with 1 you could not?
problems.answer: (b). It found something; the first only confirmed the rehearsed path.

steps.title: Explain With One Diagram
steps.mastery: Carry an explanation on a drawing you make as you speak.
steps.practice: Explain the carbon cycle while drawing it, using 6 arrows and no more than 8 words of label.
steps.detail: Drawing while speaking forces the structure out: what connects to what, and in which direction. Keep the labels down so the arrows do the work. If an arrow's direction is a guess, that is the part of the cycle you do not have, and a diagram makes it visible in a way a paragraph hides.
steps.proof: A drawing of 6 arrows whose directions you can each justify.
steps.pitfall: Drawing the diagram first and then narrating it, which lets a wrong arrow pass unnoticed.

problems.prompt: You cannot decide which way 1 of your 6 arrows points. What have you found?
problems.answer: The part of the cycle you do not actually hold, made visible by the drawing.

problems.prompt: Why draw the 6 arrows while speaking rather than drawing first and narrating after?
problems.answer: Speaking as you draw forces each arrow to be justified as it is made.

problems.prompt: State the 8-word limit this step puts on labels, and why it is there.
problems.answer: 8 words, so the arrows carry the structure instead of the text.

steps.title: Teach It Twice
steps.mastery: Re-explain a topic after fixing the gaps the first attempt exposed.
steps.practice: Fix the 2 stalls from your first attempt, then explain the same topic again inside 3 minutes.
steps.detail: The second telling is where the gain is: the first found the gaps, and an explanation that is never repeated leaves them found but unfixed. Time both attempts. A second run that is smoother but 90 seconds longer has usually added hedging rather than substance, so aim at the same length.
steps.proof: The second explanation covers the same ground in about the same time with no stall at the 2 marked points.
steps.pitfall: Rerunning the explanation without having looked up what stalled it, which rehearses the gap.

problems.prompt: Your 2nd attempt is smoother but takes 4 minutes 30 against 3 minutes. What likely changed?
problems.answer: Hedging and filler were added rather than substance.

problems.prompt: What has to happen between the 1st and 2nd attempt?
problems.answer: The 2 stalls get looked up and fixed, otherwise the gap is only rehearsed.

problems.prompt: Which shows more: (a) 1 explanation with 2 stalls, (b) 2 explanations where the 2nd has none?
problems.answer: (b). The gaps were found and then closed.

steps.title: Come With Your Own Work
steps.mastery: Arrive at a group session having already met the material alone.
steps.practice: Before 1 group session, work 6 problems alone and mark which 2 you could not finish.
steps.detail: A group is excellent for testing and explaining and useless for first exposure, because the fastest person in the room does the thinking while everybody else watches and feels productive. Arriving with 2 named sticking points means the session starts where your work stopped.
steps.proof: 6 attempted problems and 2 named sticking points, brought to the session.
steps.pitfall: Turning up to hear the topic explained, which is the one thing a group does badly.

problems.prompt: Which is a group session's best use: (a) hearing a topic explained first, (b) testing 6 problems you already attempted?
problems.answer: (b). First exposure is better done alone.

problems.prompt: You bring 2 named sticking points to a group of 4. What does that change?
problems.answer: The session starts on real difficulties instead of a general recap.

problems.prompt: Why does watching the fastest of 4 people solve a problem feel productive?
problems.answer: Following a solution resembles producing one, so recognition is mistaken for ability.

steps.title: Take Turns Explaining
steps.mastery: Rotate who explains so everybody produces rather than listens.
steps.practice: Split 4 topics between 4 people and give each person 5 minutes to explain theirs without notes.
