steps.detail: Assign the topics before the session so nobody prepares all 4. The rule that makes it work is no notes: an explanation read aloud is a recital, and the stalls are the whole point. Whoever is not explaining writes down the questions the explanation left open.
steps.proof: All 4 explained for 5 minutes each, with a list of open questions per topic.
steps.pitfall: Letting the strongest person explain 3 of the 4 topics, which is a lecture with extra chairs.

problems.prompt: In a group of 4 with 4 topics, how many explanations does each person give?
problems.answer: 1 each, for about 5 minutes.

problems.prompt: Why is explaining for 5 minutes without notes the rule?
problems.answer: Reading aloud is recital; the stalls that expose gaps only happen without notes.

problems.prompt: What do the 3 listeners do during each 5-minute explanation?
problems.answer: Write down the questions it leaves open.

steps.title: Set Each Other Problems
steps.mastery: Write a problem for somebody else and mark their answer.
steps.practice: Write 3 problems each, swap with a partner, and mark the 3 you receive against your own solutions.
steps.detail: Setting a problem requires knowing what makes it hard, and marking one requires knowing what a complete answer contains — both are more demanding than solving. Write your own solution before swapping, because a problem you cannot solve is one you cannot mark.
steps.proof: 3 problems set with solutions, and 3 received problems marked.
steps.pitfall: Setting a problem without solving it first, which produces a question nobody can mark.

problems.prompt: Why write your own solution to all 3 problems before swapping them?
problems.answer: A problem you cannot solve is one you cannot mark.

problems.prompt: Which is harder: solving 3 problems or setting 3 and marking 3?
problems.answer: Setting and marking — they need what makes a problem hard and what a full answer contains.

problems.prompt: Your partner's answer is right by a method you did not expect. What do you do?
problems.answer: Mark it right and note the method — it is a second route worth having.

steps.title: Keep the Group to Four
steps.mastery: Hold a session at a size where everybody has to contribute.
steps.practice: Run 1 session with 4 people and 1 with 8, and count how many minutes each person spoke.
steps.detail: Above about 5 the session turns into an audience: 2 people talk, the rest attend. Counting spoken minutes makes it visible rather than arguable. Four is enough for a range of approaches and small enough that silence is conspicuous.
steps.proof: Two counts of spoken minutes per person, showing how the 8-person session distributed.
steps.pitfall: Inviting everybody who asks, which produces a room where 6 people are quietly wasting an evening.

problems.prompt: In an 8-person session, 2 people speak for 40 of the 60 minutes. What has the session become?
problems.answer: An audience — 6 people are attending rather than working.

problems.prompt: Why does 4 work better than 8 for a working session?
problems.answer: Everybody has to contribute, and silence is conspicuous.

problems.prompt: How do you settle an argument about whether a group of 7 is too big?
problems.answer: Count the spoken minutes per person and look at the distribution.

steps.title: Run to a Written Agenda
steps.mastery: Fix what a session will cover before it starts.
steps.practice: Write a 4-item agenda with minutes against each, and hold the session to within 10 minutes of it.
steps.detail: Without an agenda a session spends 50 minutes on the first person's question and ends. Four items with times — 15, 15, 20, 10 — gives everybody a slot and makes overrun visible. Whoever is not explaining keeps time, which is easier than the explainer doing it.
steps.proof: The agenda with actual times beside the planned ones.
steps.pitfall: Writing 4 items with no times, which is a list rather than an agenda.

problems.prompt: An agenda plans 15, 15, 20 and 10 minutes. What is the session length?
problems.answer: 60 minutes.

problems.prompt: Item 1 takes 35 of its 15 minutes. What is the effect on the other 3?
problems.answer: They lose 20 minutes between them, so at least 1 will not happen.

problems.prompt: Why does someone other than the explainer keep time against the 4 agenda items?
problems.answer: The person explaining cannot watch the clock and the argument at once.

steps.title: Test Each Other Cold
steps.mastery: Quiz the group from cards nobody has seen in advance.
steps.practice: Bring 10 cards the others have not seen and quiz 3 people, recording who missed what.
steps.detail: Cold questions from another person are the closest a group gets to exam conditions, and they catch the material everybody quietly agreed to skip. Record the misses by person and card: a card 3 people miss is a group weakness and belongs on the next agenda.
steps.proof: A grid of 10 cards against 3 people, with the misses marked.
steps.pitfall: Circulating the cards beforehand, which turns a cold test into a rehearsal.

problems.prompt: A card is missed by 3 of 3 people. What does that mean for the next session?
problems.answer: It is a group weakness and goes on the agenda.

problems.prompt: Why must the 10 cards be unseen by the others?
problems.answer: Circulated cards make it a rehearsal rather than a test.

problems.prompt: You record misses by person only, not by card. What is lost?
problems.answer: Which material the whole group is weak on, as opposed to who is weak.

steps.title: Split and Report Back
steps.mastery: Divide reading between members and deliver it back accurately.
steps.practice: Split 4 chapters between 4 people and have each report back in 8 minutes with 3 questions for the others.
steps.detail: This only works when the reporting is tested, otherwise the group ends up with 1 person's summary of material nobody else read. Each reporter brings 3 questions on their chapter, and the others have to answer them — which is what makes a lazy report obvious immediately.
steps.proof: 4 reports of 8 minutes, each followed by 3 questions the others answered.
steps.pitfall: Accepting 4 summaries with no questions, leaving everybody with 1 chapter and 3 rumours.

problems.prompt: Why does each of the 4 reporters bring 3 questions?
problems.answer: Answering them tests whether the report actually transferred the chapter.

problems.prompt: Without questions, what does the group end up holding after 4 reports?
problems.answer: 1 chapter each and 3 second-hand summaries.

problems.prompt: 4 chapters, 8 minutes each with 3 questions apiece. Roughly how long is the session?
problems.answer: About 50 minutes with the questions included.

steps.title: End With What Changed
steps.mastery: Close a session by recording what each person will do differently.
steps.practice: Finish 1 session with each of the 4 writing 1 line on what they will work on before the next one.
steps.detail: A session that ends on "that was useful" produces nothing by Thursday. One line each, specific enough to check — "redo the 3 ratio problems I missed" — read aloud so the group has heard it. The next session opens by checking those 4 lines.
steps.proof: 4 written lines, and the next session opens by checking them.
steps.pitfall: Ending on general agreement that the topic is clearer, which cannot be checked.

problems.prompt: Which closing line is checkable: (a) "revise ratios more", (b) "redo the 3 ratio problems I missed tonight"?
problems.answer: (b). It names work that can be shown done.

problems.prompt: Why are the 4 lines read aloud rather than written privately?
problems.answer: The group has heard them, so the next session can check them.

problems.prompt: What is the first item of the next session's agenda?
problems.answer: Checking the 4 lines from last time.

steps.title: Mix Two Problem Types
steps.mastery: Alternate between 2 kinds of problem instead of blocking one kind.
steps.practice: Work 12 problems alternating quadratic factorising and simultaneous equations, 1 of each in turn.
steps.detail: Blocked practice lets you reuse the last problem's method without deciding anything, which is why it feels easy and tests little. Alternating forces the choice of method to happen every time, which is the part you will need in an exam. Expect to get more wrong than in a blocked set.
steps.proof: The 12 worked problems alternate type, and you can name the method each one needed.
steps.pitfall: Sorting the sheet into 6 of one type and 6 of the other because it runs faster that way.

problems.prompt: Which is interleaved: (a) 6 factorising then 6 simultaneous, (b) factorising and simultaneous alternating 12 times?
problems.answer: (b). Only there does the method have to be chosen each time.

problems.prompt: You score 9 out of 12 blocked and 6 out of 12 interleaved. Which set taught you more?
problems.answer: The interleaved one — the lower score is the method choice being trained.

problems.prompt: State what a blocked set of 20 identical problems stops you practising.
problems.answer: Deciding which method a problem needs, because the previous answer already settled it.

steps.title: Shuffle the Problem Set
steps.mastery: Remove the ordering cue a textbook exercise gives you for free.
steps.practice: Cut 15 exercise questions into strips, shuffle them, and work the first 8 in the order they come up.
steps.detail: A textbook exercise is grouped by the section that just taught the method, so question 7 is answered by whatever page 7 was about. Shuffling strips that cue out. Keep the answers separate so you cannot see which section a question came from while working it.
steps.proof: You worked 8 questions with no idea which section each came from, and marked them after.
steps.pitfall: Shuffling but leaving the section headings on the strips, which hands the cue back.

problems.prompt: Why is question 7 of a 20-question exercise easier than the same question in an exam?
problems.answer: It sits under the section that taught its method, so no choice of method is needed.

problems.prompt: You shuffle 15 strips but each keeps its section number. What has been lost?
problems.answer: Nothing — the section number is the cue, so it still tells you the method.

problems.prompt: Which is the better mixed set: 8 questions from 1 chapter shuffled, or 8 from 3 chapters shuffled?
problems.answer: The 3-chapter set. It mixes methods as well as order.

steps.title: Expect the Worse Score
steps.mastery: Read a lower session score as the cost of a method that lasts.
steps.practice: Record your score on 10 blocked problems and 10 interleaved ones, and write the gap between them.
steps.detail: Interleaved practice reliably scores worse on the day and better a week later, which is why almost everybody abandons it. Writing both scores down turns that into a number you expected rather than evidence you are getting worse. Compare again after a week on the same material.
steps.proof: You have 2 scores and a gap, and can say which one predicts next week's performance.
steps.pitfall: Going back to blocked practice after 2 sessions because the score dropped, which is the effect working.

problems.prompt: You score 8 out of 10 blocked and 5 out of 10 interleaved today. Which predicts next week better?
problems.answer: The interleaved 5 — blocked scores measure the method being fresh, not retained.

problems.prompt: State the usual reason people give up on interleaving after 2 sessions.
problems.answer: The session score falls, which looks like getting worse and is the effect working.

problems.prompt: How would you test the claim after 7 days?
problems.answer: Work 10 fresh mixed problems from the same material and compare with the blocked group's score.

steps.title: Interleave Across Topics
steps.mastery: Mix problems from 3 topics so the topic itself has to be identified.
steps.practice: Build a 12-problem set drawing 4 each from trigonometry, logarithms and sequences, shuffled.
steps.detail: Mixing methods inside one topic is the easy version; mixing topics means the first decision is what kind of problem this even is. Keep a tally of which topic you misidentify, because that is a different error from getting the method wrong once you know the topic.
steps.proof: The set holds 4 problems from each topic in mixed order, with misidentifications tallied separately.
steps.pitfall: Grouping the 3 topics into blocks of 4 within the set, which rebuilds the cue.

problems.prompt: Name the 2 different errors a 3-topic mixed set separates.
problems.answer: Misidentifying the topic, and choosing the wrong method once the topic is known.

problems.prompt: You misidentify 3 of 12 problems' topics. What does that point at?
problems.answer: The cues that mark a problem as trigonometry rather than sequences, which is its own thing to study.

problems.prompt: Why is a set of 12 drawn from 3 topics harder than 12 from 1 topic shuffled?
problems.answer: The topic has to be identified first, which a single-topic set decides for you.

steps.title: Alternate Within a Session
steps.mastery: Rotate subjects inside 1 study block without losing the thread of either.
steps.practice: Run a 60-minute block as 3 rotations of 20 minutes across 2 subjects, ending on the harder one.
steps.detail: Switching has a cost, so the slices need to be long enough to get into the work — 20 minutes rather than 5. Write 1 line at each switch saying where you stopped, so the next rotation starts from the work instead of from re-reading. End on the subject you find harder, while the block still has your attention.
steps.proof: The block held 3 rotations, each with a hand-off line, and finished on the harder subject.
steps.pitfall: Slicing a 60-minute block into 6 switches of 10 minutes, where the switching costs more than the mixing gains.

problems.prompt: A 60-minute block covers 2 subjects. Is 3 rotations of 20 minutes or 6 of 10 the better split?
problems.answer: 3 of 20. At 10 minutes the switching costs more than the mixing gains.

problems.prompt: What goes in the 1-line hand-off written at each switch?
problems.answer: Where you stopped, so the next rotation resumes the work instead of rereading.

problems.prompt: Why end a 60-minute block on the harder subject rather than the easier one?
problems.answer: The harder work gets attention while some is left, rather than the last 20 minutes being spent on the easy subject.

steps.title: Mixed Paper Every Week
steps.mastery: Sit a mixed set weekly as the measure of what has actually held.
steps.practice: Build a 20-question mixed paper from the last 4 weeks and sit it in 45 minutes without notes.
steps.detail: This is the check on everything else: cards, blocked practice and rereading all flatter you, and a mixed paper across 4 weeks does not. Mark it hard, then tally the misses by topic — the topic with most misses is next week's opening work, whatever the schedule said.
steps.proof: A marked 20-question paper with the misses tallied by topic.
steps.pitfall: Building the paper from this week only, which makes it a test of what is freshest.

problems.prompt: Should the weekly mixed paper draw from this week or the last 4 weeks?
problems.answer: The last 4 weeks, so it tests what held rather than what is freshest.

problems.prompt: Your 20-question paper shows 5 misses in sequences and 1 elsewhere. What changes next week?
problems.answer: Next week opens on sequences, regardless of what the schedule had planned.

problems.prompt: Why is a mixed paper a better measure than a score of 18 out of 20 on today's cards?
problems.answer: Cards test single facts while fresh; the paper tests choosing methods across 4 weeks of material.

steps.title: Keep One Summary Page
steps.mastery: Retain a single page per subject worth reopening in a year.
steps.practice: Reduce 1 finished subject to 1 page holding its 8 main results, and file it where you will find it.
steps.detail: After an exam most material is discarded and the subject becomes something you once did. One page changes that: 8 results, the 2 or 3 organising ideas, and nothing else. File the pages together by subject so the whole set is 1 folder rather than 6 notebooks.
steps.proof: 1 page per subject, holding its main results, filed in 1 place.
steps.pitfall: Keeping all 60 pages of notes, which is the same as keeping none because nobody reopens 60 pages.

problems.prompt: Which is more likely to be reopened in 12 months: 60 pages of notes or 1 page of 8 results?
problems.answer: The 1 page — 60 pages is functionally the same as keeping nothing.

problems.prompt: What belongs on the 1 page besides the 8 results?
problems.answer: The 2 or 3 organising ideas, and nothing more.

problems.prompt: Why file all the subject pages together rather than 1 per notebook?
problems.answer: The whole set becomes 1 folder you can actually open.

steps.title: Review Once a Month
steps.mastery: Revisit a finished subject briefly at monthly intervals.
steps.practice: Put 4 monthly 20-minute reviews in the calendar for 1 finished subject, and keep the first one.
steps.detail: Twenty minutes a month is enough to keep a subject retrievable, which is a fraction of what relearning it costs. Work from the 1-page summary: cover it, produce what you can, then check. Put the dates in the calendar, because a review with no date does not happen once the deadline has gone.
steps.proof: 4 dated reviews in the calendar and the first one done.
steps.pitfall: Planning to review "now and then", which is how a subject quietly disappears over 6 months.

problems.prompt: How long is each of the 4 monthly reviews, and what does it work from?
problems.answer: 20 minutes, worked from the 1-page summary with the page covered.

problems.prompt: Why must the 4 reviews carry dates?
problems.answer: Without a deadline pushing them, undated reviews do not happen.

problems.prompt: Compare 20 minutes a month against relearning a subject from scratch.
problems.answer: The monthly review is a small fraction of the cost of relearning.

steps.title: Test It, Do Not Reread
steps.mastery: Make a maintenance review a retrieval attempt rather than a read.
steps.practice: Cover your 1-page summary and produce 6 of its 8 results from memory before looking.
steps.detail: The maintenance review has the same rule as everything else: produce first, check second. Rereading a page you wrote is comfortable, fast and nearly worthless. Aim at 6 of 8 — below that the subject needs a longer session, above it the interval can stretch.
steps.proof: A count of how many of the 8 results you produced before uncovering the page.
steps.pitfall: Reading the page over twice and calling it a review.

problems.prompt: You produce 3 of 8 results from memory. Stretch the interval or run a longer session?
problems.answer: Run a longer session — 3 of 8 means the subject is fading.

problems.prompt: You produce 8 of 8. What can change?
problems.answer: The interval can stretch, to 2 months or more.

problems.prompt: Why is rereading your own 1-page summary nearly worthless as a review?
problems.answer: It tests recognition of your own handwriting rather than recall of the content.

steps.title: Use It on Something Real
steps.mastery: Apply a finished subject to a problem outside the course.
steps.practice: Find 1 use for a finished subject outside its course and spend 30 minutes on it.
steps.detail: Nothing maintains a subject like using it: statistics on a dataset you care about, a language on a menu, mechanics on a bicycle. Thirty minutes of real use is worth several reviews, because it forces the parts you skipped and shows which ones you never actually had.
steps.proof: 30 minutes of the subject applied outside the course, with 1 line on what it exposed.
steps.pitfall: Waiting for a use to come up naturally, which for most subjects is never.

problems.prompt: Name 1 real use of basic statistics outside a course, doable in 30 minutes.
problems.answer: Summarising a dataset you care about — a mean, a spread and what they say.

problems.prompt: Why is 30 minutes of real use worth more than 3 reviews?
problems.answer: It forces the parts you skipped and exposes what you never actually had.

problems.prompt: What do you write down after the 30 minutes?
problems.answer: One line on what the use exposed as missing.

steps.title: Stretch the Intervals
steps.mastery: Lengthen maintenance gaps as a subject proves durable.
steps.practice: Move a subject from monthly to 3-monthly reviews after 3 consecutive reviews scoring 7 of 8 or better.
steps.detail: Maintenance should get cheaper. The rule is evidence-based rather than a feeling: 3 consecutive good scores earn a longer gap. A single weak review sends it back to monthly, which is cheap insurance against losing a subject you thought was safe.
steps.proof: A record of 3 review scores and the interval they earned.
steps.pitfall: Stretching to 6 months after 1 good review, which is usually where a subject is lost.

problems.prompt: How many consecutive reviews at 7 of 8 earn a longer interval?
A 3-monthly subject scores 4 of 8. What happens to the interval?
problems.answer: It goes back to monthly.

problems.prompt: Why is stretching to 6 months after 1 good review risky?
problems.answer: One score is not evidence of durability, and that is usually where a subject is lost.

steps.title: Refresh Before You Need It
steps.mastery: Rebuild a dormant subject in advance of the thing that needs it.
steps.practice: Pick a subject you will need in 8 weeks and schedule 4 sessions of 45 minutes before then.
steps.detail: A subject needed for a course, a job or an interview is best rebuilt on a schedule rather than in a panic the week before. Four sessions: 1 to test what remains, 2 on the gaps, 1 to apply it. Starting from the 1-page summary makes the first session a measurement rather than a guess.
steps.proof: 4 dated sessions, the first of which measured what remained.
steps.pitfall: Leaving the refresh to the week it is needed, which is relearning under pressure.

problems.prompt: How are the 4 refresh sessions divided?
problems.answer: 1 to test what remains, 2 on the gaps, 1 to apply it.

problems.prompt: Why does session 1 work from the 1-page summary?
problems.answer: It measures what actually remains instead of guessing at it.

problems.prompt: You leave an 8-week refresh until the final week. What have you converted it into?
problems.answer: Relearning under pressure, which costs more and holds less.

steps.title: Notice What You Lost
steps.mastery: Identify which parts of a subject decayed and which held.
steps.practice: Compare a review score by section against your score 6 months ago and name the 2 weakest sections.
steps.detail: Decay is uneven: procedures you used stay, definitions you memorised go first, and anything you never derived goes fastest. Comparing by section rather than in total tells you which kind of material you lose, which changes how you learn the next subject.
steps.proof: A section-by-section comparison and the 2 weakest named.
steps.pitfall: Comparing totals, which hides that 1 section carried all the loss.

problems.prompt: Which usually decays fastest: a procedure you used 40 times or a definition you memorised once?
problems.answer: The memorised definition.

problems.prompt: Your total score fell 3 marks but 1 of 6 sections lost all 3. What does the total hide?
problems.answer: That the loss is concentrated in 1 section rather than spread.

problems.prompt: A pattern of losing memorised definitions should change what about the next 8 topics?
problems.answer: More of it gets derived rather than memorised.

steps.title: Teach It Once a Year
steps.mastery: Explain a finished subject to somebody as a durable annual test.
steps.practice: Explain 1 finished subject for 15 minutes to somebody who does not know it, once a year.
steps.detail: Teaching is the hardest maintenance test and the cheapest to arrange: it needs the structure, the joins and the reasons, all of which decay silently. Fifteen minutes to a real person exposes more than an hour of private review, and their questions are the part you cannot anticipate.
steps.proof: A 15-minute explanation given, with the questions you could not answer written down.
steps.pitfall: Explaining it to somebody who already knows it, who will fill the gaps for you without either of you noticing.

problems.prompt: Why explain to somebody who does not know the subject rather than to 1 who does?
problems.answer: Someone who knows it fills the gaps for you without either of you noticing.

problems.prompt: What is worth writing down from the 15 minutes?
problems.answer: The questions you could not answer.

problems.prompt: Why does teaching test more than 1 hour of private review?
problems.answer: It needs structure, joins and reasons, which decay silently and cannot be faked aloud.

steps.title: Keep the Folder Alive
steps.mastery: Maintain the whole set of retained subjects as one small system.
steps.practice: Audit your folder of 1-page summaries, giving each subject a next-review date and dropping 1 you no longer want.
steps.detail: A retention system with 12 subjects in it and no dates is a drawer. Every page gets a next date and a current interval; anything you genuinely do not intend to keep gets dropped on purpose rather than by neglect. Twenty minutes, twice a year.
steps.proof: Every page in the folder carries a next-review date, and 1 has been deliberately dropped.
steps.pitfall: Keeping 12 subjects nominally alive and reviewing 2, which loses the other 10 without ever deciding to.

problems.prompt: Your folder holds 12 subjects and you review 2. What is happening to the other 10?
problems.answer: They are being lost by neglect rather than by a decision.

problems.prompt: What does every page in a 12-subject folder carry after the audit?
problems.answer: A next-review date and its current interval.

problems.prompt: Is the folder audited twice a year or every 2 weeks, and for how long?
problems.answer: Twice a year, about 20 minutes.

steps.title: First-Letter Mnemonics
steps.mastery: Build a sentence whose initials recover an ordered list.
steps.practice: Make a mnemonic for the 7 colours of the spectrum in order: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet.
steps.detail: Take the initials — R O Y G B I V — and build a sentence whose words start with them in order. Make it concrete and slightly odd, because bland sentences do not stick. Test it by writing the 7 colours from the sentence alone an hour later.
steps.proof: The sentence returns all 7 colours in the right order an hour later.
steps.pitfall: Building a mnemonic with 2 words starting with the same letter, so the order goes ambiguous.

problems.prompt: Give the initials your mnemonic must cover for the spectrum's 7 colours in order.
problems.answer: R, O, Y, G, B, I, V.

problems.prompt: Your mnemonic for 5 items has 2 words beginning with S. What breaks?
problems.answer: The order between those 2 items, since the initials no longer distinguish them.

problems.prompt: Why does a slightly absurd 7-word sentence hold better than a plain one?
problems.answer: Odd images are recalled more reliably than bland ones.

steps.title: Numbers Into Images
steps.mastery: Convert an arbitrary number into a picture you can recall.
steps.practice: Turn the year 1453 into 1 concrete image and recall it correctly an hour later.
steps.detail: Split the number into pairs — 14 and 53 — and give each pair a fixed image you reuse across all dates. Join the 2 images into 1 scene involving the event. The pairing has to stay fixed across every number you learn, or the images collide.
steps.proof: You can state 1453 from the image, and the image from the event.
steps.pitfall: Inventing fresh images per number, which is as much to remember as the digits were.

problems.prompt: Split 1815 into the 2 pairs this method uses.
Why must the image for the pair 53 stay the same across every date you learn?
problems.answer: Otherwise images collide and no number can be read back reliably.

problems.prompt: You built 6 fresh images for 6 dates. What is the problem?
problems.answer: 6 new images is as much to store as the 12 digits were.

steps.title: Walk a Memory Palace
steps.mastery: Place items along a familiar route and collect them in order.
steps.practice: Place 10 items along a route through your home, 1 per location, then recall all 10 in order.
steps.detail: Pick a route you know without thinking and fix the order of its 10 stops before placing anything. Put 1 item at each stop, interacting with it oddly rather than sitting beside it. Walk the route in your head twice immediately, then once again an hour later.
steps.proof: You can recite the 10 items in route order, and backwards.
steps.pitfall: Placing 2 items at 1 stop, which is where a palace usually loses something.

problems.prompt: How many items go at each of the 10 stops, and why?
problems.answer: 1. Two at a stop is where the route loses an item.

problems.prompt: Why should the route be fixed before any of the 10 items are placed?
problems.answer: The order of the stops is what supplies the order of the items.

problems.prompt: You can recall 10 items forwards but not backwards. What does that suggest?
problems.answer: The items are chained to each other rather than anchored to the 10 stops.

steps.title: Link a Chain of Facts
steps.mastery: Join a short sequence with images so each item pulls the next.
steps.practice: Chain the 5 stages of mitosis by linking each to the next with 1 vivid image.
steps.detail: A chain suits sequences of 5 to 8 where the order matters and the items are related. Link consecutive pairs, making each junction do something physical. The weakness is that a broken link loses the tail, so test by starting from the middle as well as the top.
steps.proof: You can give the 5 stages from stage 1 and from stage 3.
steps.pitfall: Building 1 long story where a forgotten junction takes the whole rest of the chain with it.

problems.prompt: Why test a 5-item chain by starting from item 3 as well as item 1?
problems.answer: To check the tail survives a broken junction rather than depending on the whole chain.

problems.prompt: Which suits a chain better: 6 ordered stages, or 40 unordered vocabulary words?
problems.answer: The 6 ordered stages — chains carry order and break down at length.

problems.prompt: State the failure mode of a 20-item chain.
problems.answer: One forgotten junction loses every item after it.

steps.title: Use It for the Arbitrary Only
steps.mastery: Choose memory techniques for material no reasoning can recover.
steps.practice: Sort 10 items into 2 lists — arbitrary and derivable — and build images for the arbitrary ones only.
steps.detail: Mnemonics are expensive to build, so they belong on names, symbols, dates and conventions. Anything derivable is cheaper to reconstruct than to encode, and a palace full of derivable facts is effort spent hiding the reasoning you should have learned.
steps.proof: Images exist for the arbitrary list only, and you can derive every item on the other one.
steps.pitfall: Building a mnemonic for a formula you could derive in 3 lines.

problems.prompt: Mnemonic or derivation for the symbol "K" for potassium?
problems.answer: Mnemonic — it comes from kalium and cannot be reasoned out.

problems.prompt: Mnemonic or derivation for the area of a trapezium, and does it take about 3 lines or 30?
problems.answer: Derivation — it follows from splitting the shape, in about 3 lines.

problems.prompt: Why is a memory palace holding 30 derivable formulas a poor use of it?
problems.answer: Each could be rebuilt from reasoning, so the encoding effort buys nothing.

steps.title: Test the Mnemonic Cold
steps.mastery: Check a mnemonic still returns its content after a day away.
steps.practice: Recall 3 mnemonics built yesterday and write out what each unpacks to, unprompted.
steps.detail: A mnemonic can feel solid the minute it is built and be gone by the next day, usually because it was abstract or too similar to another one. Test cold, with nothing in front of you. Where it fails, rebuild the image more concretely rather than repeating the old one.
steps.proof: 3 mnemonics recalled and unpacked correctly with nothing in view.
steps.pitfall: Testing the mnemonic while looking at the list it encodes, which proves nothing.

problems.prompt: A mnemonic built yesterday returns nothing today. Repeat it 10 times or rebuild the image?
problems.answer: Rebuild it more concretely — repetition of a weak image stays weak.

problems.prompt: Why test 3 mnemonics with the encoded list out of sight?
problems.answer: With the list visible the test measures recognition, not recall.

problems.prompt: Name the 2 usual reasons a fresh mnemonic fails within 24 hours.
problems.answer: It was too abstract, or too similar to another one you already use.

steps.title: Keep the Palace Stocked
steps.mastery: Maintain a set of routes and know what currently occupies each.
steps.practice: List your 3 routes and what each is holding, and clear 1 that is finished with.
steps.detail: Routes are reusable but not simultaneously, so leaving an exam's content in a route blocks it for the next subject. Keep an index card per route saying what is in it and when it was loaded. Clearing a route means walking it once deliberately empty before reloading.
steps.proof: 3 routes indexed with their contents, and 1 walked empty.
steps.pitfall: Loading a new list into a route that still holds an old one, which mixes the 2 sets.

problems.prompt: You load a 2nd list of 10 items into a route still holding the 1st. What happens?
problems.answer: The 2 sets interfere and neither reads back cleanly.

problems.prompt: What goes on the index card for each of the 3 routes?
problems.answer: What it holds and when it was loaded.

problems.prompt: How is 1 route cleared before its 10 stops are reused?
problems.answer: Walk its 10 stops once deliberately empty before loading anything new.

steps.title: Keep an Error Log
steps.mastery: Record every wrong answer in one place with what went wrong.
steps.practice: Start a 3-column log — problem, what I did, what was wrong — and enter 5 errors from your last set.
steps.detail: The third column is the one that matters and the one people leave out: not the right answer, but the specific move that failed. "Multiplied instead of divided in the ratio step" is an entry you can act on; "got it wrong" is not. Keep 1 log for the whole subject so patterns are visible.
steps.proof: 5 entries, each naming a specific wrong move rather than a wrong answer.
steps.pitfall: Writing the correct solution in column 3, which records the answer and loses the diagnosis.

problems.prompt: Which is a usable column-3 entry: (a) "the answer was 42", (b) "divided by the 3 : 2 ratio the wrong way round"?
problems.answer: (b). It names the move that failed.

problems.prompt: Why keep 1 log for a subject rather than 5 logs per topic?
problems.answer: Patterns across topics only show up when the errors sit together.

problems.prompt: You log 5 errors and 4 say "careless". What is wrong with the log?
problems.answer: "Careless" is not a diagnosis — each needs the specific step that went wrong.

steps.title: Sort Slip From Gap
steps.mastery: Tell an execution slip apart from something you did not know.
steps.practice: Label each of your 5 logged errors S for slip or G for gap, and count the 2 totals.
steps.detail: They need different fixes: a gap is studied, a slip is prevented by a check. Redo the problem immediately — if you now get it right without learning anything, it was a slip. Counting the 2 totals tells you whether to spend the week on content or on checking procedures.
steps.proof: 5 labelled errors and 2 totals you can state.
steps.pitfall: Calling a gap a slip because you understood the solution when you read it.

problems.prompt: You redo a missed problem immediately and get it right with no new learning. Slip or gap?
problems.answer: A slip — the knowledge was there and the execution failed.

problems.prompt: Of 10 errors, 7 are gaps. Does the week go on content or on checking?
problems.answer: On content, since most losses are things not known.

problems.prompt: Why is "I understood the solution when I read it" not evidence of a slip?
problems.answer: Following a solution is recognition; it does not show you could have produced it.

steps.title: Redo It From Blank
steps.mastery: Rework a missed problem from a blank page after the fix.
steps.practice: Redo 3 logged problems from blank paper 1 day later, with the log and solution shut.
steps.detail: Reading your own correction is not the same as being able to produce the solution, and the gap between those 2 is where repeat mistakes live. A day's delay is deliberate: it stops you reproducing the correction from short-term memory rather than from understanding.
steps.proof: 3 problems reworked correctly from blank paper, a day after the correction.
steps.pitfall: Redoing the problem 2 minutes after reading the solution, which tests the last 2 minutes only.

problems.prompt: Why wait a day before redoing a corrected problem rather than 2 minutes?
problems.answer: A 2-minute gap tests short-term memory of the correction, not the method.

problems.prompt: You redo 3 problems and miss 1 again. What happens to that entry?
problems.answer: It goes back in the log as a gap and is studied from the source, not redone again.

problems.prompt: Which shows the fix worked: (a) rereading your correction, (b) producing the solution from blank paper a day later?

steps.title: Count the Repeat Offenders
steps.mastery: Find the error you keep making across weeks of work.
steps.practice: Tally your log by error type and name the 1 type with the most entries over 3 weeks.
steps.detail: Individual errors feel like bad luck; a tally shows they are not. Group by the failing move — sign errors, ratio inversions, dropped units — and count. The top type is usually responsible for a surprising share of lost marks, and it is 1 thing to fix rather than twenty.
steps.proof: A tally by type, with the top type named and its count.
steps.pitfall: Grouping by topic rather than by failing move, which hides an error that crosses topics.

problems.prompt: Your 3-week tally shows 11 sign errors, 4 ratio inversions and 3 others. Where does the week go?
problems.answer: On sign handling, which is over half the losses.

problems.prompt: Why group 18 logged errors by failing move rather than by topic?
problems.answer: The same move fails across topics, and a topic grouping splits it into small piles.

problems.prompt: What does a log with 18 single-entry types suggest about the grouping?
problems.answer: The categories are too fine — the entries need grouping into fewer failing moves.

steps.title: Write the Prevention Rule
steps.mastery: Turn a repeated error into a check you run every time.
steps.practice: Write 2 one-line checks for your top error type, such as "circle every minus sign before expanding".
steps.detail: A rule has to be an action at a specific moment, not an intention. "Be careful with signs" changes nothing; "circle every minus sign before expanding" happens at a point in the work where it can be done. Two rules maximum, so they actually get used.
steps.proof: 2 checks, each naming an action and the moment it happens.
steps.pitfall: Writing 6 rules, which means none of them is running by Thursday.

problems.prompt: Which is a usable rule: (a) "be careful with units", (b) "write the unit beside every number before adding"?
problems.answer: (b). It names an action at a moment.

problems.prompt: Why cap the list at 2 rules?
problems.answer: More than 2 stops being run, so the rules become intentions again.

problems.prompt: Write a 1-line check for repeatedly inverting a 3 : 2 ratio.
problems.answer: Before multiplying, say aloud which quantity is getting bigger.

steps.title: Mark Like the Examiner
steps.mastery: Apply a mark scheme to your own work without giving yourself the benefit.
steps.practice: Mark 3 of your worked answers against a published mark scheme, awarding only what is written on the page.
steps.detail: Marking your own work generously is the fastest way to a nasty surprise. Award marks only for what is on the paper: no credit for what you meant, knew, or would have written with more time. Where you lose a mark for presentation rather than content, that is worth logging too.
steps.proof: 3 scores from the mark scheme, with the lost marks itemised.
steps.pitfall: Awarding the method mark because you knew the method, when the page does not show it.

problems.prompt: You knew a method but did not write it, and the scheme gives 2 method marks. What do you award?
problems.answer: 0. The scheme pays for what is on the page.

problems.prompt: Why itemise the 4 lost marks rather than recording a total of 12 out of 16?
problems.answer: The items say what to fix; the total says only how it felt.

problems.prompt: A mark is lost for no units in the final line of a 6-mark answer. Content or presentation, and worth logging?
problems.answer: Presentation, and yes — it is a cheap, repeatable loss.

steps.title: Close the Log Weekly
steps.mastery: Clear an error log every week so it stays a worklist rather than a diary.
steps.practice: Go through last week's 12 entries and close each one: redone, studied, or rule written.
steps.detail: An open entry is work outstanding, and a log that only grows is a record of failure rather than a tool. Each Friday, every entry gets closed with a mark saying how, or is carried forward once. An entry carried twice is a sign the fix is bigger than the log and needs a study session of its own.
steps.proof: Last week's entries all closed or carried once, with the count of each.
steps.pitfall: Letting the log grow to 60 entries, at which point nobody opens it again.

problems.prompt: Of 12 entries, 9 are closed and 3 carried forward for the 2nd time. What do the 3 need?
problems.answer: A study session of their own — the fix is bigger than a log entry.

problems.prompt: Why close the log weekly rather than letting it reach 50 entries?
problems.answer: A log of 50 unclosed entries stops being opened, so the work never gets done.

problems.prompt: Name the 3 ways an entry can be closed.
problems.answer: Redone from blank, studied from the source, or turned into a prevention rule.

steps.title: Sit One Under Timed Conditions
steps.mastery: Reproduce the exam's conditions closely enough to feel them.
steps.practice: Sit 1 past paper in 90 minutes with no notes, no phone and no pauses, at a desk.
steps.detail: Familiarity is what takes the edge off, and it only comes from the real thing: timer running, materials away, no stopping for a cup of tea. Do it at the time of day the exam falls if you can. The first one will feel worse than the exam did in your imagination, which is the point.
steps.proof: 1 completed paper, sat unbroken in 90 minutes with nothing to hand.
steps.pitfall: Pausing the timer for 5 minutes to look 1 thing up, which removes the condition being practised.

problems.prompt: You pause the timer for 5 minutes during a 90-minute mock. What has been lost?
problems.answer: The time pressure, which was the condition being practised.

problems.prompt: Why sit a 90-minute mock at the same time of day as the real exam?
problems.answer: The state you will be in is part of what is being made familiar.

problems.prompt: Name the 3 things that must be away during a timed mock.
problems.answer: Notes, phone and any pauses.

steps.title: Write the Blank Plan
steps.mastery: Have a written procedure for the moment nothing comes.
steps.practice: Write 3 steps to follow if you go blank, such as breathing, moving to question 4, and returning after 10 minutes.
steps.detail: Going blank is a state, and a decision made inside it is unreliable — so make the decision now, in writing, and follow it rather than thinking. Three steps at most: something physical, something procedural, and a time to come back. Rehearse it once in a mock so it is familiar.
steps.proof: 3 written steps, rehearsed once under timed conditions.
steps.pitfall: Planning to "stay calm and think it through", which is not a procedure and cannot be followed.

problems.prompt: Which is a usable blank plan: (a) stay calm and focus, (b) 4 slow breaths, move to question 4, return in 10 minutes?
problems.answer: (b). It is a sequence you can follow without deciding anything.

problems.prompt: Why decide the 3 steps in advance rather than in the moment?
problems.answer: Decisions made while blank are unreliable, so the procedure is made beforehand.

problems.prompt: What are the 3 kinds of step the plan holds?
problems.answer: Something physical, something procedural, and a time to return.

steps.title: Practise the First Five Minutes
steps.mastery: Rehearse the opening of a paper until it needs no decisions.
steps.practice: Rehearse the same 5-minute opening 3 times: write your name, scan all questions, mark times, start question 1.
steps.detail: The worst nerves are in the first few minutes, so make those minutes a routine rather than a set of choices. The same 4 actions in the same order, practised 3 times, means the paper is under way before there is anything to panic about.
steps.proof: The same 4-action opening carried out 3 times in 5 minutes.
steps.pitfall: Opening by reading question 1 closely, which means the paper's shape is still unknown 10 minutes in.

problems.prompt: Name the 4 actions of the rehearsed opening, in order.
problems.answer: Name on the paper, scan every question, mark finish times, start question 1.

problems.prompt: Why scan all the questions before starting question 1?
problems.answer: So the paper's shape and the time plan are known before any writing.

problems.prompt: Why rehearse the opening 3 times rather than reading about it?
problems.answer: Under nerves a practised routine runs where a remembered intention does not.

steps.title: Slow the Breathing Down
steps.mastery: Bring physical arousal down with a technique that works while seated.
steps.practice: Practise 6 cycles of 4 seconds in and 6 seconds out, seated, and take your pulse before and after.
steps.detail: A longer out-breath than in-breath reliably slows the heart, and 1 minute of it is enough to change the state. Practise it away from the exam so it is automatic. Taking the pulse before and after gives you evidence it works, which matters on the day you doubt it.
steps.proof: A pulse figure before and after 1 minute of the pattern.
steps.pitfall: Trying it for the first time in the exam hall, where an unfamiliar technique is 1 more thing to worry about.

problems.prompt: 6 cycles of 4 seconds in and 6 out takes how long?
problems.answer: 1 minute.

problems.prompt: In a 4-seconds-in, 6-seconds-out cycle, why is the out-breath the longer one?
problems.answer: A longer exhale slows the heart rate rather than raising it.

problems.prompt: Why take a pulse before and after the 1 minute?
problems.answer: It gives evidence the technique works, for the day you doubt it.

steps.title: Run the Worst Case
steps.mastery: State what would actually happen in the outcome you fear.
steps.practice: Write 3 sentences describing what follows if this exam goes badly, including the resit or retake route.
steps.detail: Unexamined, the fear has no shape and therefore no size. Written out — a resit in 4 months, a different offer, a year that looks different — it is usually survivable and always finite. This is not positive thinking: it is making the cost specific enough to stop being unbounded.
steps.proof: 3 written sentences naming what follows, including a route forward.
steps.pitfall: Refusing to think about it at all, which leaves the fear at whatever size it wants to be.

problems.prompt: Why write the worst case in 3 sentences rather than avoiding the thought?
problems.answer: Unexamined, the fear has no size; written down it is finite and usually survivable.

problems.prompt: What must the 3 sentences include besides the bad outcome?
problems.answer: The route forward from it, such as a resit or a different offer.

problems.prompt: Is writing the 3 worst-case sentences the same as telling yourself it will be fine?
problems.answer: No — it makes the cost specific rather than denying it.

steps.title: Keep the Routine Boring
steps.mastery: Fix the hours before an exam so nothing new happens in them.
steps.practice: Write the 6 things you will do in the 3 hours before the exam, in order, and change none of them on the day.
steps.detail: Novelty raises arousal, so the morning should be the one you have already had several times: same breakfast, same route, same arrival margin, same 1 page of notes. Deciding it in advance also removes 6 small decisions from a morning that has no capacity for them.
steps.proof: 6 written items in order, and the same list used in a mock morning.
steps.pitfall: Cramming a new topic in the last hour, which raises arousal and displaces what you had ready.

problems.prompt: Is reading 1 new topic in the last hour a good idea?
problems.answer: No — it raises arousal and displaces material you already had ready.

problems.prompt: Why write the 6 items in advance?
problems.answer: It removes 6 decisions from a morning with no capacity for them.

problems.prompt: Of the 6 fixed items, which may be read in the final hour before the exam?
problems.answer: The 1 page of summary you have already used, and nothing new.

steps.title: Handle the Hard Question
steps.mastery: Move on from a question that has stalled without losing the paper.
steps.practice: Set a 2-minute rule in a mock: if a question has not started in 2 minutes, mark it and move to the next.
steps.detail: A stalled question is expensive twice — the minutes and the state it puts you in. Mark it with a star, move on, and come back with the paper mostly done and the panic gone. Most people find 1 or 2 starred questions are straightforward on the second visit.
steps.proof: A mock paper with starred questions, all revisited before the end.
steps.pitfall: Staying on question 3 for 18 minutes because giving up on it feels like failing.

problems.prompt: A question has not started after 2 minutes. What do you do?
problems.answer: Star it, move to the next question, and return later.

problems.prompt: Why is 18 minutes on a stalled question expensive twice?
problems.answer: It costs the minutes and leaves you in a worse state for the rest of the paper.

problems.prompt: What often happens on the 2nd visit to a starred question?
problems.answer: It is straightforward, because the paper is mostly done and the panic has gone.

steps.title: Sleep the Night Before
steps.mastery: Protect the last night's sleep as part of the preparation.
steps.practice: Set a finish time 2 hours before bed for 3 nights running and record what time you actually slept.
steps.detail: An hour of revision at midnight costs more than it adds, because recall and time management both degrade with lost sleep. Stop 2 hours before bed and do something undemanding. Practise it for 3 nights rather than only the night before, since a single early night rarely works on command.
steps.proof: 3 recorded sleep times after a 2-hour wind-down.
steps.pitfall: Revising until 1am the night before, which trades 2 marks of content for a worse morning.

problems.prompt: Why practise the wind-down for 3 nights rather than only the night before?
problems.answer: A single early night rarely works on command, so the pattern needs establishing.

problems.prompt: What does 1 hour of revision at midnight cost?
problems.answer: More than it adds — recall and time management both degrade with lost sleep.

problems.prompt: Revision stops how long before bed — 2 hours or 20 minutes?
problems.answer: 2 hours.

steps.title: Debrief Your Own Nerves
steps.mastery: Record what the state actually did to your performance, and adjust.
steps.practice: After a timed mock, write 3 lines on what nerves cost you: time, blanks, or rushed reading.
steps.detail: The point is to make it specific. If you lost 6 marks to misreading 2 questions, the fix is the underlining routine, not calmness in general. If you lost 10 minutes to a stall, the fix is the 2-minute rule. Nerves you can attribute to a mechanism are nerves you can work on.
steps.proof: 3 lines naming what the state cost and which routine addresses it.
steps.pitfall: Concluding only that you were nervous, which points at no change.

problems.prompt: You lost 6 marks to misreading 2 questions. Which routine is the fix?
problems.answer: The underlining of command words and constraints.

problems.prompt: You lost 10 minutes to a stall on question 3. Which routine is the fix?
problems.answer: The 2-minute rule for starring and moving on.

problems.prompt: Why is "I was nervous" not a usable debrief line?
problems.answer: It names no mechanism, so it points at no change.

steps.title: Notes in Your Own Words
steps.mastery: Restate a source's sentence in your own wording without losing what it claims.
steps.practice: Rewrite this in under 12 words: "Cellular respiration converts glucose and oxygen into ATP, carbon dioxide and water."
steps.detail: Read the sentence, look away from it, then write what it said. Looking away is the whole trick — with the sentence in view you will copy its structure and change 2 words. Check afterwards that nothing was dropped: the inputs, the outputs and the direction all have to survive.
steps.proof: Your version is shorter, shares few words with the original, and still names glucose and oxygen going in and ATP coming out.
steps.pitfall: Swapping synonyms while keeping the sentence shape, which is copying with extra steps.

problems.prompt: Restate in under 10 words: "Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level."
problems.answer: Prices across the economy keep climbing over time.

problems.prompt: Which is a note in your own words: (a) "Respiration converts glucose plus oxygen to ATP, CO2 and water", (b) "Cells burn sugar with oxygen to make energy, giving off CO2 and water"?
problems.answer: (b). The first only swapped a word or two of the original.

problems.prompt: A 40-word paragraph became a 38-word note. State what has gone wrong.
problems.answer: Nothing was compressed, so the note is a transcription rather than a note.

steps.title: Two-Column Note Page
steps.mastery: Split a page so cues sit apart from the material they recover.
steps.practice: Rule a page 1 third to 2 thirds, put 8 cue questions on the left and their answers on the right.
steps.detail: The narrow left column holds only questions or keywords; the wide right holds the substance. Nothing on the left may give the answer away, because the left column is what you will read with the right covered. Leave 4 lines at the foot of the page for a summary written after the session.
steps.proof: With the right column covered, the 8 cues alone tell you what the page held.
steps.pitfall: Writing statements rather than questions on the left, so covering the right proves nothing.

problems.prompt: Turn the note "The Treaty of Versailles imposed 132 billion marks in reparations" into a left-column cue.
problems.answer: How much did Versailles demand in reparations?

problems.prompt: Which cue is usable: (a) "Reparations: 132 billion marks", (b) "How large were the reparations?"
problems.answer: (b). The first states the answer, so covering the right column tests nothing.

problems.prompt: A page holds 8 cues and you recover 5 answers. What goes in the summary at the foot?
problems.answer: The 3 you could not recover, named so the next session starts there.

steps.title: Compress to a Line
steps.mastery: Reduce a page of notes to the one sentence that carries its point.
steps.practice: Take 1 page of notes and write a single sentence under 20 words that a reader could rebuild the page from.
steps.detail: Write the sentence after the page is finished, not during. Ask what the page would still be true without, and drop that first. If the sentence needs 2 clauses joined by and, the page probably covered 2 things and wants splitting in half.
steps.proof: Reading your sentence a week later brings the page's argument back.
steps.pitfall: Listing the page's topics instead of saying what it claims about them.

problems.prompt: Compress to under 15 words: notes covering supply, demand, and how price settles where the 2 curves meet.
problems.answer: Price settles at the quantity where what sellers offer matches what buyers will take.

problems.prompt: Which is a compression: (a) "Supply, demand, equilibrium, surplus, shortage", (b) "Price moves until the amount offered equals the amount wanted"?
problems.answer: (b). The first is a list of headings, not a claim.

problems.prompt: Your 1-sentence summary needs 2 clauses joined by "and". What does that suggest about the page?
problems.answer: It covered 2 separate points and should be split into 2 pages with 1 summary each.

steps.title: Mark the Gaps
steps.mastery: Flag on the page itself the places where your notes stopped making sense.
steps.practice: Go through 1 set of notes and put a "?" beside every line you could not explain to somebody in 30 seconds.
steps.detail: Do this the same day, while you still remember which lines you wrote confidently and which you copied. A question mark is a promise to come back, so each one needs either an answer or a deletion within the week — a page of unanswered marks is a page you have learned to skip.
steps.proof: Every line on the page is either explainable or carries a "?".
steps.pitfall: Marking nothing because the notes look familiar, which confuses recognising your handwriting with understanding it.

problems.prompt: You can read a line of your notes but not explain it. What does the line get?
problems.answer: A question mark, answered or deleted within the week.

problems.prompt: Which page is in better shape: (a) 20 clean lines, none marked, (b) 20 lines with 4 marked "?"
problems.answer: (b). It knows where its 4 weak points are.

problems.prompt: A page carries 11 marks out of 14 lines. State what to do with the page.
problems.answer: Rewrite it from the source — the notes were copied rather than understood.

steps.title: Notes You Reuse
steps.mastery: Return to a page of notes and leave it better than you found it.
steps.practice: Reopen 1 page from last week, answer its 2 oldest "?" marks and add 1 link to another page.
steps.detail: A note you never reopen was a transcription with extra steps. Each visit should change the page: an answered mark, a tighter summary line, a cross-reference to the page that explains it. Date each change in the margin so you can see which pages get used and which you have been avoiding.
steps.proof: The page has fewer marks than last week and 1 new link on it.
steps.pitfall: Rewriting the page neatly instead of answering what it got stuck on.

problems.prompt: A page has been reopened 4 times with no change to it. What does that tell you?
problems.answer: It is being reread rather than used, so nothing on it is being fixed.

problems.prompt: Which counts as a reuse: (a) copying the page out neatly, (b) answering 2 of its "?" marks and linking it to the page that explains them?
problems.answer: (b). Neatness changes nothing the page got wrong.

problems.prompt: You have 12 pages and only 3 have margin dates. State what the other 9 are.
problems.answer: Pages written once and never used, which is the failure this step exists to catch.

steps.title: Identify Upcoming Assignments
steps.mastery: List all assignments and their due dates within the next month.
steps.practice: Write down the due date and required pages for Assignment 1, due in 12 days, covering pages 45‑60.
steps.detail: Open your course syllabus or online portal. Locate every assignment that falls within the next 30 days. For each, note the exact number of days until it is due and copy the page range or topic that must be covered. Record this information in a simple table so you can refer to it later when you start planning your study time.
steps.proof: The list shows Assignment 1: due in 12 days, pages 45‑60.
steps.pitfall: Missing the exact due‑day count or writing the wrong page range.

problems.prompt: What is the due‑day count for Assignment 1?
List the page range for Assignment 1.
If Assignment 1 is due in 12 days, on which calendar day (counting today as day 0) must it be submitted?
problems.answer: Day 12.
problems.hint: Add the due‑day count to today.

steps.title: Calculate Study Load
steps.mastery: Convert each assignment into total study minutes needed.
steps.practice: Estimate 30 minutes per 5 pages and compute minutes for Assignment 1 (pages 45‑60).
steps.detail: Decide on a realistic reading‑and‑note‑taking speed, such as 30 minutes for every 5 pages of textbook. Count the pages required for the assignment, divide by 5, then multiply by 30 to get the total minutes you will need. Write the result next to the assignment in your table so you have a clear time target.
steps.proof: 15 pages × 30 min/5 pages = 90 minutes.
steps.pitfall: Using the wrong pages‑to‑time ratio or forgetting to multiply.

problems.prompt: Calculate study minutes for Assignment 1 which has 15 pages, using 30 minutes per 5 pages.
problems.answer: 90 minutes.

problems.prompt: Using 30 minutes per 5 pages, how many minutes are required for Assignment 1 (pages 45‑59)?
problems.answer: 90 minutes.

problems.prompt: If you mistakenly used 25 minutes per 5 pages for the 15‑page Assignment 1, what incorrect total would you obtain?
problems.answer: 75 minutes.
problems.hint: Apply the wrong ratio to the 15 pages.

steps.title: Create Daily Slots
steps.mastery: Allocate specific study blocks each day to meet the total minutes before the due date.
steps.practice: Schedule three 30‑minute blocks on days 1, 3, and 5 leading up to Assignment 1.
steps.detail: Look at your personal calendar for the next 5 days. Choose three separate days that are free enough to host a focused 30‑minute session. Write the day numbers and the length of each block next to the assignment entry. Ensure the total of the blocks equals the minutes you calculated in the previous step.
steps.proof: Sum of blocks = 90 minutes, matching the needed time.
steps.pitfall: Over‑booking a day or leaving a day empty when minutes remain.

problems.prompt: How many minutes are in one 30‑minute study block?
problems.answer: 30 minutes.

problems.prompt: If you schedule three 30‑minute blocks on days 1, 3, 5, what is the total study minutes scheduled?
problems.answer: 90 minutes.

problems.prompt: If you add a fourth 30‑minute block on day 2, what total minutes would you have scheduled?
problems.answer: 120 minutes.

steps.title: Build a Mini‑Schedule
steps.mastery: Arrange the study blocks in chronological order with clear start times.
steps.practice: Write a schedule: Day 1 09:00‑09:30, Day 3 14:00‑14:30, Day 5 19:00‑19:30 for Assignment 1.
steps.detail: Take the days you selected and assign a concrete start time for each 30‑minute block. Use a 24‑hour or AM/PM format consistently. Record the three entries in a notebook or digital calendar so you can see the order and avoid double‑booking. Verify that the total time adds up to the required 90 minutes.
steps.proof: The three entries cover 90 minutes before the 12‑day deadline.
steps.pitfall: Confusing AM/PM or writing overlapping times.

problems.prompt: What is the start time of the Day 1 study block in the schedule?
How many total minutes are covered by the three schedule entries (each 30 minutes)?
problems.answer: 90 minutes.

problems.prompt: If the Day 3 block is moved to 13:30‑14:00, does it overlap with the Day 5 block at 19:00‑19:30?
problems.answer: No.

steps.title: Review and Adjust
steps.mastery: Check progress after each block and shift remaining blocks if needed.
steps.practice: After Day 1, note 30 minutes completed; move the Day 5 block to Day 4 to keep a buffer.
steps.detail: At the end of each study session, tick off the minutes you actually finished. If a block was missed or ran short, relocate the remaining time to an earlier day to maintain a safety margin before the deadline. Update your written schedule each time you make a change so the plan always reflects reality.
steps.proof: Total completed 30 min, remaining 60 min scheduled for Days 3 and 4.
steps.pitfall: Failing to update the schedule after a missed block.

problems.prompt: After completing the Day 1 block, how many minutes have been finished?
problems.answer: 30 minutes.

problems.prompt: After moving the Day 5 block to Day 4, how many minutes remain scheduled for Days 3 and 4 combined?
problems.answer: 60 minutes.

problems.prompt: If the Day 3 block is missed, how can you redistribute the remaining 60 minutes into two 30‑minute blocks on Days 4 and 5 to meet the deadline?
problems.answer: Schedule a 30‑minute block on Day 4 and another on Day 5.

steps.title: Cover the Solution
steps.mastery: Attempt a problem with the worked answer physically out of sight.
steps.practice: Fold the page so the solution is hidden and attempt 1 problem for 5 minutes before checking.
steps.detail: Reading a worked solution and following it feels like problem-solving and is closer to reading. Folding the page, or covering it with a card, makes the attempt unavoidable. Give it a fixed 5 minutes so the attempt has an end, then check in full rather than line by line.
steps.proof: A 5-minute attempt on paper, made before the solution was seen.
steps.pitfall: Glancing at the first line of the solution "to get started", which supplies the only decision that mattered.

problems.prompt: Which is problem practice: (a) reading 6 worked solutions, (b) attempting 3 problems with the solutions covered?
problems.answer: (b). Only the covered attempt makes you choose the method.

problems.prompt: You read the 1st line of a solution to get started. What has been given away?
problems.answer: The choice of method, which is usually the whole difficulty.

problems.prompt: Why fix the attempt at 5 minutes rather than working until it is solved?
problems.answer: It bounds the struggle so checking happens, and marks how far you got unaided.

steps.title: Write the Method First
steps.mastery: Name the method a problem needs before any working is done.
steps.practice: Write 1 line naming the method for 6 problems, without solving any of them.
steps.detail: Separating the choice from the execution trains the part exams actually test. For each problem write something like "factorise, then set each bracket to 0". Six of these takes 5 minutes and shows whether the difficulty is choosing or computing — which are 2 different things to practise.
steps.proof: 6 named methods, and you can say which of the 6 you were unsure about.
steps.pitfall: Starting the algebra while writing the plan, which merges the 2 skills again.

problems.prompt: Name the method for: solve x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0.
problems.answer: Factorise into (x - 2)(x - 3), then set each bracket to 0.

problems.prompt: Name the method for: find the angle in a right triangle with opposite 3 and hypotenuse 5.
problems.answer: Use sine: angle = arcsin(3/5).

problems.prompt: You name all 6 methods correctly but get 3 wrong when solving. Which skill needs the work?
problems.answer: Execution — the method choice is already sound.

steps.title: Check Before Marking
steps.mastery: Test your own answer for sense before comparing it with the book.
steps.practice: Substitute your answer back into 3 problems and confirm each satisfies the original equation.
steps.detail: Substitution, units and rough size catch most errors without the answer key. For x = 4 in x^2 - 5x + 4 = 0, put 4 back and see 16 - 20 + 4 = 0. Doing this first means the key confirms your check rather than replacing it, and you keep the habit for an exam where there is no key.
steps.proof: 3 answers verified by substitution before the key was opened.
steps.pitfall: Going straight to the answers, which trains you to need them.

problems.prompt: Check x = 4 in x^2 - 5x + 4 = 0.
problems.answer: 16 - 20 + 4 = 0, so it satisfies the equation.

problems.prompt: You calculate a speed of 3000 m/s for a cyclist. What does the sense check say?
problems.answer: It is far too large — about 3 orders of magnitude out, so the working has an error.

problems.prompt: Why substitute before opening the answer key, in under 20 words?
problems.answer: It builds the check you will need in an exam, where no key exists.

steps.title: Work to the Last Line
steps.mastery: Finish a problem completely rather than stopping when the route is clear.
steps.practice: Take 4 problems you would abandon once the method is obvious and carry each to a final numeric answer.
steps.detail: Stopping at "I know how to do this" hides the arithmetic slips, the sign errors and the simplification that is actually where marks go. Carry all 4 to a boxed final value with units, then mark them. Expect at least 1 of the 4 to be wrong despite the method being right.
steps.proof: 4 boxed final answers with units, marked right or wrong.
steps.pitfall: Counting a problem as done at the point you can see the route, which is where most marks are lost.

problems.prompt: You see the method for 4 problems and complete none. How many marks would that score in an exam?
problems.answer: Only the method marks — usually 1 or 2 of each question's total.

problems.prompt: Of 4 problems where the method was right, 1 comes out wrong. What does that number tell you?
problems.answer: That about a quarter of your losses are execution, not understanding.

problems.prompt: What are the 2 things a final answer must carry?
problems.answer: The value and its units.

steps.title: Attempt Above Your Level
steps.mastery: Spend a bounded stretch on a problem you may not solve.
steps.practice: Spend 12 minutes on 1 problem a level above your usual, recording each thing you tried.
steps.detail: A problem you cannot do is where the learning is densest, and the record is what turns it from wasted time into work: 3 lines saying what you tried and why each stopped. After 12 minutes, read the solution and compare it against your list to see which of your attempts was closest.
steps.proof: A list of what you tried, and 1 line saying which attempt the solution resembled.
steps.pitfall: Giving a hard problem an hour, which costs the rest of the session for 1 question.

problems.prompt: Why bound a hard attempt at 12 minutes rather than working until it yields?
problems.answer: An unbounded attempt eats the session for 1 question, and the record is what carries the value.

problems.prompt: After 12 minutes you have 3 failed attempts written down. What do you do with them?
problems.answer: Compare them against the solution and see which was closest and why it stopped.

problems.prompt: Which is more use: 1 hard problem with 3 recorded attempts, or 8 routine problems solved?
problems.answer: The hard one, provided the attempts were recorded — that is where new method comes from.

steps.title: Time a Set of Ten
steps.mastery: Work a set under the clock at roughly exam pace.
steps.practice: Work 10 routine problems in 20 minutes, marking the clock time beside each as you finish it.
steps.detail: Pace is a separate skill from method, and the only way to find yours is to measure it. Writing the time beside each answer shows where you slowed: 1 problem eating 7 of the 20 minutes is the thing to study, and it is invisible if you only record the total.
steps.proof: 10 answers with times beside them, totalling about 20 minutes.
steps.pitfall: Stopping the clock to look something up, which makes the pace figure meaningless.

problems.prompt: 10 problems in 20 minutes gives what average per problem?
problems.answer: 2 minutes each.

problems.prompt: 1 of your 10 problems took 7 minutes. What does the per-problem timing show that a total cannot?
problems.answer: Which single problem type is costing the pace.

problems.prompt: You pause the clock to look up a formula. What has the timing become?
problems.answer: Meaningless as a pace figure, because the exam will not pause.

steps.title: Build Your Own Problem
steps.mastery: Write a problem of a given type and solve it correctly.
steps.practice: Write 2 quadratic problems with integer roots, then solve them and check the roots are what you intended.
steps.detail: To set a problem you have to work backwards from the answer, which uses the method in reverse and exposes gaps that solving does not. Start from the roots — say 3 and -5 — expand to get x^2 + 2x - 15, then solve your own expression and confirm the roots come back.
steps.proof: 2 problems whose solutions return the roots you started from.
steps.pitfall: Writing a problem with roots that are not integers by accident, then assuming your solving was wrong.

problems.prompt: Build a quadratic with roots 3 and -5.
Build a quadratic with roots 2 and 2, and say what is special about it.
problems.answer: (x - 2)^2 = x^2 - 4x + 4, a repeated root.

problems.prompt: Why does writing a problem expose gaps that solving 10 does not?
problems.answer: It runs the method backwards, which needs the structure rather than the procedure.

steps.title: Survey Before Reading
steps.mastery: Map a chapter's structure from its headings before reading a word of the body.
steps.practice: Take a 20-page chapter and write out its 6 headings, 2 figure captions and the summary box, in 4 minutes.
steps.detail: Read only what is in bold or large type, plus anything in a box. Write the headings down the left of a page as a list, leaving 3 blank lines under each. That list is the skeleton you will hang the reading on, and the blank lines are where the answers go.
steps.proof: You can say what the chapter covers, in order, without having read a paragraph.
steps.pitfall: Drifting into reading the first paragraph properly, which turns a 4-minute survey into 20 minutes.

problems.prompt: A chapter runs 18 pages with 5 headings and 3 figures. How many lines does your skeleton hold before you start reading?
problems.answer: 8 — one per heading and one per figure caption.

problems.prompt: Which of these belongs in a survey: (a) the chapter summary, (b) the third paragraph of section 2, (c) the bold key terms?
problems.answer: (a) and (c). The paragraph is body text and waits until the reading pass.

problems.prompt: You surveyed a 30-page chapter in 12 minutes. State what went wrong and what the target was.
problems.answer: 12 minutes is a reading pass, not a survey; 30 pages of headings and boxes should take about 5 minutes.

steps.title: Turn Headings Into Questions
steps.mastery: Convert a heading into the question the section answers, so reading has a target.
steps.practice: Rewrite these 3 headings as questions: "Enzyme Inhibition", "The Marshall Plan", "Big-O Notation".
steps.detail: Put what, why or how in front of the heading and finish the sentence. "Enzyme Inhibition" becomes "How is an enzyme stopped from working, and by what?". A heading you cannot make a question of is one you do not yet know the shape of, which is itself worth noticing.
steps.proof: Each of your 3 questions can be answered in a sentence once the section is read.
steps.pitfall: Writing a question so broad — "What is this section about?" — that any paragraph answers it.

problems.prompt: Turn the heading "Diminishing Returns" into a question worth reading for.
problems.answer: Why does each extra unit of input give less output, and where does the turn happen?

problems.prompt: Which is the better reading question for "The Krebs Cycle": (a) What is the Krebs cycle about? (b) What goes into the Krebs cycle and what comes out?
problems.answer: (b). It names what an answer must contain, so you can tell when you have found it.

problems.prompt: A section is headed "Results". Write 2 questions for it that a heading that vague cannot answer on its own.
problems.answer: Results of what measurement, and did they support the hypothesis?

steps.title: Read for the Answers
steps.mastery: Read a section hunting the answer to your own question rather than sentence by sentence.
steps.practice: Read 1 section with your question above it and stop at the sentence that answers it; mark that sentence with a bracket.
steps.detail: Keep the question visible at the top of the page. When you reach the answering sentence, bracket it and write the answer in your own words in the blank lines under the heading. If you finish the section without finding an answer, the question was wrong — rewrite it before moving on.
steps.proof: Every question on your skeleton has a bracketed sentence and a one-line answer under it.
steps.pitfall: Highlighting as you go instead of answering, which leaves a yellow page and no answers.

problems.prompt: You have read 4 pages of a section and found no answer to your question. What are the 2 possible causes?
problems.answer: The question was wrong for that section, or the answer is later in a part you have not reached.

problems.prompt: Which page is better evidence of reading to learn: (a) 30 highlighted lines, (b) 5 bracketed sentences with 5 answers written beside them?
problems.answer: (b). Highlighting records where you were; the written answers record what you got.

problems.prompt: A 6-heading chapter leaves you 6 answers of about 15 words each. How many words of notes is that, and what should they cover?
problems.answer: About 90 words, covering the answer to every question the chapter's headings raise.

steps.title: Recite Without Looking
steps.mastery: Say a section's answer aloud with the book shut, before reading the next one.
steps.practice: Close the book at the end of 1 section and say its answer aloud in under 30 seconds.
steps.detail: Do this at the section boundary rather than at the end of the chapter, while the material is still recoverable and the gap is still cheap to fix. Where the recitation stalls, open the book at that point only, read the 2 or 3 sentences you needed, and say it again from the top.
steps.proof: You can give the section's answer aloud twice running with the book shut.
steps.pitfall: Reciting with the page in view, which tests recognition rather than recall.

problems.prompt: A chapter has 6 sections. How many recitations does this step ask for, and when?
problems.answer: 6 — one at the end of each section, before the next one is read.

problems.prompt: You stall halfway through reciting section 3. What is the next action: (a) reread section 3 whole, (b) open it at the stall, read 2 sentences, recite again?
problems.answer: (b). Reread only the gap, then test the whole thing again.

problems.prompt: Why is reciting at the end of each section better than one recitation at the end of a 6-section chapter?
problems.answer: The gaps are found while they are still cheap to fix, and each section is tested while it can still be recalled.

steps.title: Review the Whole Chapter
steps.mastery: Rebuild a chapter's argument from your own skeleton a day after reading it.
steps.practice: Cover your notes a day after reading and rebuild the chapter's 6 answers from the headings alone.
steps.detail: Work from the heading list with the answers covered. Write what you can, then uncover and mark what you missed with a dot. Two dots on the same answer over two reviews means the material never went in, and that answer is what tomorrow's session opens with rather than the next chapter.
steps.proof: You can produce the chapter's answers from its headings, and the dots show which 1 or 2 need another pass.
steps.pitfall: Rereading the notes instead of covering them, which feels like review and tests nothing.
